prompt_engineering.title: Prompt Engineering & LLM Workflows
prompt_engineering.description: Design, test, and improve prompts and multi-step LLM workflows for useful, verifiable outcomes.

modules.title: How LLMs Actually Respond
modules.description: Build a practical mental model of language models, context, tokens, and prompt structure.
modules.story: A support team asks a model to summarize a long customer thread, but each rewrite changes what the model notices.
modules.discovery: Compare the model's answer when the same request has different context, wording, and constraints.

lessons.title: A Language Model Predicts What Comes Next
lessons.objective: Explain how next-token prediction produces fluent text without guaranteeing truth.
lessons.concept: An LLM estimates likely next tokens from patterns learned during training. It generates a continuation, not a database lookup, so plausible wording can still be incorrect.
lessons.example: Ask for a summary of a short fictional support ticket, then change one key fact and observe which details the model preserves.
lessons.challenge: Write two possible continuations for an ambiguous opening sentence and identify what context would disambiguate them.
lessons.takeaway: Fluency is evidence of language patterning, not proof that a claim is true.

lessons.title: Tokens, Context Windows, and Lost Details
lessons.objective: Estimate how context limits and tokenization affect long requests.
lessons.concept: Text is split into tokens that may be words, word pieces, or punctuation. The context window holds instructions, conversation, and output; important details can be crowded out when it fills.
lessons.example: Give a model a long meeting transcript with a specific decision near the beginning, then ask for that decision after adding unrelated notes.
lessons.challenge: Compress a 500-word brief to a smaller set of decision-critical facts and test whether the answer remains grounded in them.
lessons.takeaway: Manage context deliberately; more text is not automatically more useful.

modules.title: Prompt Patterns
modules.description: Use examples, roles, context, tasks, constraints, and formats to shape model behavior.
modules.story: A product team needs consistent release notes from tickets written by different engineers.
modules.discovery: Observe how examples and explicit output requirements reduce variation between responses.

lessons.title: Zero-Shot and Few-Shot Requests
lessons.objective: Choose between a direct instruction and a small set of examples.
lessons.concept: Zero-shot prompting gives an instruction without examples. Few-shot prompting supplies representative input-output pairs so the model can infer a pattern, while examples must cover meaningful edge cases.
lessons.example: Classify three sample bug reports as usability, reliability, or performance issues, then compare direct instructions with two labeled examples.
lessons.challenge: Create a few-shot prompt for sorting five fictional feedback comments and include one example that tests an ambiguous boundary.
lessons.takeaway: Examples teach a pattern; they do not replace a clear task definition.

lessons.title: Role, Context, Task, and Constraints
lessons.objective: Separate audience context, requested work, and rules in a reusable prompt.
lessons.concept: A useful prompt makes the role or perspective, relevant context, task, constraints, and expected format explicit. Each part removes a different source of ambiguity.
lessons.example: Turn a vague request to explain an outage into a request for a customer-safe summary with known facts, prohibited speculation, and three labeled sections.
lessons.challenge: Rewrite a weak prompt using role, context, task, constraints, and output format; ask a peer to identify any remaining ambiguity.
lessons.takeaway: Prompt structure clarifies intent, but output still needs review.

modules.title: Reliable LLM Workflows
modules.description: Break work into verifiable steps and handle structured output, ambiguity, and iteration.
modules.story: An analyst receives mixed-format survey notes and needs a decision-ready summary without fabricated figures.
modules.discovery: Compare one large request with a sequence of smaller steps that expose assumptions and checks.

lessons.title: Break a Task into Verifiable Steps
lessons.objective: Decompose a multi-part request into stages with inspectable outputs.
lessons.concept: A workflow separates input preparation, extraction, transformation, and final drafting. Intermediate results make errors easier to locate and allow deterministic checks before a later model call.
lessons.example: Extract claims from interview notes, attach source quotes, group claims by theme, then draft a summary from the reviewed groups.
lessons.challenge: Design a four-step workflow for turning product feedback into prioritized themes, specifying what a person verifies at each step.
lessons.takeaway: Small steps make model work easier to inspect and correct.

lessons.title: Structured Outputs and Validation
lessons.objective: Specify a machine-readable response and validate its required fields and values.
lessons.concept: A format instruction can request JSON or a fixed schema, but the response still needs parsing and validation. Check required keys, types, allowed values, and whether each claim is supported by input.
lessons.example: Request JSON with issue_type, urgency, and evidence_quote, then reject responses with a missing quote or an unknown issue type.
lessons.challenge: Write a schema for a support-ticket triage result and list three invalid responses your validator should reject.
lessons.takeaway: A structured-looking response is not valid until it passes checks.

modules.title: From Prompt to Workflow
modules.description: Turn a one-off prompt into a reusable, human-supervised workflow.
modules.story: A small operations team repeats the same research task every week and needs consistent handoffs.
modules.discovery: Identify which parts should be templated, which context changes, and where a person should approve work.

lessons.title: Reusable Templates and Context Management
lessons.objective: Create a prompt template with explicit variables and a bounded context package.
lessons.concept: Templates separate stable instructions from changing inputs. A compact context package should include relevant source material, dates, definitions, and exclusions while avoiding unrelated history.
lessons.example: Build a weekly report template with variables for reporting period, source table, audience, and metric definitions.
lessons.challenge: Convert a repeated research prompt into a template and mark every variable that must be supplied or checked before use.
lessons.takeaway: Reusable prompts need controlled inputs and versioned instructions.

lessons.title: Human-in-the-Loop Prompt Chains
lessons.objective: Place review gates where an error could change a decision or reach a user.
lessons.concept: A prompt chain passes one step's output into another. Human review is useful at uncertain or consequential boundaries, such as approving extracted facts before drafting or sending an external action.
lessons.example: A draft customer reply is generated from a ticket, checked against a policy excerpt, and held for agent approval before sending.
lessons.challenge: Map a two-prompt chain and add a review checkpoint with a clear accept, edit, or stop condition.
lessons.takeaway: Automation should stop for review when confidence or impact makes unchecked continuation unsafe.

modules.title: Build a Practical LLM Workflow
modules.description: Plan, test, improve, and document a small LLM workflow around a real task.
modules.story: Your team wants to turn incoming project briefs into concise, traceable kickoff notes.
modules.discovery: Run the same workflow on varied inputs and find where quality changes, rather than judging it from one polished example.

lessons.title: Test and Improve a Workflow
lessons.objective: Use representative cases and failure cases to improve a prompt without hiding regressions.
lessons.concept: A small evaluation set should include typical, incomplete, conflicting, and out-of-scope inputs. Compare outputs against explicit criteria and change one prompt element at a time.
lessons.example: Test a brief summarizer on a complete brief, one missing a deadline, and one containing contradictory dates.
lessons.challenge: Create five test cases for a workflow, score factual support and completeness, then make one revision and rerun all cases.
lessons.takeaway: A prompt change is an experiment; check its effect across cases.

lessons.title: Document a Reusable LLM Workflow
lessons.objective: Deliver a workflow specification another person can run and audit.
lessons.concept: A practical handoff records the task boundary, inputs, prompt version, output format, validation rules, human review point, known limits, and escalation path.
lessons.example: Document a meeting-note workflow that cites transcript sections, flags missing owners, and never invents due dates.
lessons.challenge: Package your workflow with one sample input, expected output, validator checklist, and a short list of known failure modes.
lessons.takeaway: A workflow is ready to share when its limits and checks are as clear as its prompt.

ai_automation_n8n.title: AI Automation with n8n
ai_automation_n8n.description: Build maintainable n8n workflows that connect events, APIs, AI model calls, and human decisions.

modules.title: Automation Thinking
modules.description: Choose good automation boundaries and model inputs, decisions, actions, and exceptions.
modules.story: A small team manually copies form submissions into a tracker, then sends a follow-up email.
modules.discovery: Trace the work from trigger to result and separate repeatable rules from decisions that need a person.

lessons.title: Map a Workflow Before Automating
lessons.objective: Represent a routine process as a trigger, steps, decisions, outputs, and exception paths.
lessons.concept: Automation works best when inputs and outcomes are observable. Map the happy path and the exceptions before choosing nodes; unclear processes become unclear workflows.
lessons.example: A new request triggers validation, assigns a category, creates a tracker item, and notifies an owner only when required fields are present.
lessons.challenge: Draw a workflow for processing a support request and mark which steps are deterministic and which require judgment.
lessons.takeaway: Understand the work before automating its clicks.

lessons.title: Choose a Safe First Automation
lessons.objective: Assess value, failure impact, data sensitivity, and reversibility before building.
lessons.concept: A useful first automation is frequent, bounded, and easy to review. Estimate time saved alongside failure cost, permissions, and the ability to undo or correct an action.
lessons.example: Automatically label an internal draft for review before considering an automation that sends customer messages.
lessons.challenge: Score three candidate tasks by frequency, error impact, data sensitivity, and reversibility; justify the safest pilot.
lessons.takeaway: Start where an error is visible and recoverable.

modules.title: n8n Fundamentals
modules.description: Build and inspect workflows using triggers, nodes, connections, and execution data.
modules.story: You are creating a workflow that turns a test webhook into a normalized task record.
modules.discovery: Watch data move node by node and use execution output to explain each transformation.

lessons.title: Triggers, Nodes, and Connections
lessons.objective: Build a simple n8n workflow and explain how execution passes between nodes.
lessons.concept: A trigger starts an execution; action and transformation nodes consume incoming items and emit new items. Connections define flow, while node settings define what happens to each item.
lessons.example: Start with a manual trigger, add a Set node for title and owner, then inspect the output JSON.
lessons.challenge: Build a three-node workflow that receives a sample task, adds a priority field, and outputs a normalized object.
lessons.takeaway: Inspect each node's input and output before adding more complexity.

lessons.title: Expressions, Items, and Execution History
lessons.objective: Reference incoming fields and diagnose a workflow using saved execution data.
lessons.concept: n8n passes items containing JSON data. Expressions read values from prior nodes; execution history lets you compare expected and actual item shapes when a field is absent or renamed.
lessons.example: Map `customer.email` into a notification node and handle a missing email without stopping unrelated items.
lessons.challenge: Use a sample payload with one missing field, add a guarded expression or validation branch, and verify both paths in execution history.
lessons.takeaway: Data shape is part of the workflow contract.

modules.title: APIs, Webhooks, and Data
modules.description: Connect external services with secure requests, clear payloads, and deliberate data transformations.
modules.story: A form provider sends a webhook, and the team needs to enrich the submission from an internal API.
modules.discovery: Inspect the incoming request and decide what must be validated before data crosses a service boundary.

lessons.title: Receive Webhooks and Validate Payloads
lessons.objective: Accept a webhook payload and reject or route malformed input safely.
lessons.concept: A webhook exposes an endpoint that receives an event. Validate its structure, required values, and authenticity where available before using its data or triggering side effects.
lessons.example: Require a request ID and email field, then route missing values to an error log rather than the normal processing path.
lessons.challenge: Create a webhook test payload, add a validation branch for a missing required field, and capture a useful failure reason.
lessons.takeaway: Treat incoming webhook data as untrusted input.

lessons.title: Call APIs and Transform Responses
lessons.objective: Make an authenticated API request and map its response into a stable workflow shape.
lessons.concept: API calls need the right method, headers, query or body, and error handling. Transform responses into a stable internal shape so later nodes do not depend on incidental provider fields.
lessons.example: Fetch a task record, map provider-specific `display_name` to `owner_name`, and retain the original record ID for traceability.
lessons.challenge: Call a test API, map three response fields into a normalized object, and route a non-success status to a separate branch.
lessons.takeaway: Normalize data at integration boundaries.

modules.title: Connecting AI Models
modules.description: Add model calls with bounded context, explicit output contracts, and privacy-aware inputs.
modules.story: An operations workflow needs to summarize free-text submissions before a human triages them.
modules.discovery: Decide what the model needs, what it must not receive, and what the workflow can verify after the response.

lessons.title: Add an AI Model Call
lessons.objective: Configure a model step with a narrow task and only necessary input data.
lessons.concept: An AI node is a service call inside a workflow. Keep instructions explicit, scope the context to the task, avoid unnecessary personal data, and record enough metadata to diagnose the result.
lessons.example: Send a redacted request description to produce a two-sentence summary and a suggested category, not an automatic final decision.
lessons.challenge: Add a model step to a sample workflow, redact a sensitive field, and inspect the prompt and returned data.
lessons.takeaway: A model node should have a defined job and bounded access to data.

lessons.title: Parse and Check Model Output
lessons.objective: Validate AI output before downstream nodes use it.
lessons.concept: Model output can be malformed, incomplete, or unsupported. Parse the expected structure, check allowed values and evidence, and route invalid output to a review or retry path with limits.
lessons.example: Accept only one of four category labels and require a short source quote before creating a suggested ticket tag.
lessons.challenge: Create a parser and validation branch that sends an invalid model response to a human review queue.
lessons.takeaway: Never let an unchecked model response silently become workflow truth.

modules.title: AI-Powered Workflows
modules.description: Combine deterministic steps and AI suggestions into useful automation patterns.
modules.story: A team wants to classify incoming documents and create a draft action list without losing source traceability.
modules.discovery: Separate model-assisted interpretation from deterministic updates and externally visible actions.

lessons.title: Combine Rules with AI Suggestions
lessons.objective: Use fixed validation and routing around a model-generated suggestion.
lessons.concept: Deterministic rules are appropriate for required fields, permissions, and thresholds. AI can help interpret open text; workflow logic should bound and verify the result before applying it.
lessons.example: Check file type and sender first, ask a model to suggest a document category, then route low-evidence cases to review.
lessons.challenge: Design a hybrid workflow where rules validate inputs and the AI suggests a label, with a review path for uncertain cases.
lessons.takeaway: Use AI for ambiguity and rules for explicit requirements.

lessons.title: Preserve Sources and Audit Decisions
lessons.objective: Carry source identifiers and decision reasons through an automated workflow.
lessons.concept: Traceability links a generated suggestion to the input that produced it. Keep stable IDs, relevant excerpts, model or prompt version, and the final human decision where appropriate.
lessons.example: Store a document ID and the paragraph supporting a generated action item beside the draft task.
lessons.challenge: Add source ID and evidence fields to a workflow result and verify they survive each transformation node.
lessons.takeaway: A useful AI workflow can explain where its output came from.

modules.title: Memory, Conditions, and Human Approval
modules.description: Manage state explicitly and put approval gates before consequential actions.
modules.story: An assistant prepares supplier follow-ups, but a person must approve commitments before they leave the company.
modules.discovery: Identify the state a later step needs and which action must pause for approval.

lessons.title: Conditions and Explicit Workflow State
lessons.objective: Route executions with clear conditions and retain only the state needed for later steps.
lessons.concept: Branches should be based on explicit, testable values. Memory is application state that must be scoped, updated, and expired deliberately; chat history alone is not a reliable business record.
lessons.example: Store a request ID and approval status in a table, then continue only when the status becomes approved.
lessons.challenge: Add approved, rejected, and missing-status branches to a workflow and test one input for each.
lessons.takeaway: Represent workflow state explicitly instead of assuming the model remembers it.

lessons.title: Add a Human Approval Gate
lessons.objective: Pause a workflow for review before sending or changing important information.
lessons.concept: A human approval step presents the proposed action, its source, and a clear choice. Define timeout, rejection, and edit behavior so an unanswered request does not become approval.
lessons.example: Show a proposed supplier email and its source facts to an owner; send only after an explicit approve event.
lessons.challenge: Design an approval gate with approve, edit, reject, and timeout outcomes and test each path.
lessons.takeaway: Approval must be an explicit event, not the absence of an objection.

modules.title: Reliability and Error Handling
modules.description: Make failures observable, retries bounded, and repeated events safe to process.
modules.story: A downstream service times out after a workflow has already created one task.
modules.discovery: Determine which failures can be retried and how to prevent a retry from duplicating an action.

lessons.title: Retries, Timeouts, and Error Paths
lessons.objective: Add bounded retry and failure handling to an external service step.
lessons.concept: Transient failures may succeed on retry; invalid input and permission errors usually will not. Use timeouts, a retry limit, backoff where supported, and an error path that preserves context for investigation.
lessons.example: Retry a rate-limited request twice, but route a 403 response directly to an access-error queue.
lessons.challenge: Configure a test workflow with a retry limit and error branch; simulate one transient error and one permanent error.
lessons.takeaway: Retries need limits and a reason.

lessons.title: Idempotency and Duplicate Events
lessons.objective: Prevent repeated webhook deliveries from repeating an irreversible action.
lessons.concept: At-least-once delivery means an event can arrive more than once. Use a stable event ID or idempotency key to check whether work was already completed before creating another external effect.
lessons.example: Store processed invoice event IDs and skip a second delivery of the same event.
lessons.challenge: Add a deduplication check to a webhook flow and submit the same event twice; confirm only one action is created.
lessons.takeaway: Design for duplicate delivery instead of assuming exactly-once execution.

modules.title: Build an AI Automation
modules.description: Ship an end-to-end automation that receives, interprets, decides, acts, and reports.
modules.story: A team receives a daily stream of requests and wants faster triage while keeping a person in control.
modules.discovery: Build from a small test set, then trace one request from event to final report.

lessons.title: Assemble the End-to-End Workflow
lessons.objective: Connect a trigger, validation, AI processing, a bounded action, and a result report.
lessons.concept: A dependable automation has a defined input contract, explicit processing stages, guarded side effects, and a report containing outcome and trace ID. Each stage should be testable independently.
lessons.example: Receive a request, validate required fields, summarize text, suggest a route, request human approval, then report the action and event ID.
lessons.challenge: Build the workflow with a test webhook and fake destination; demonstrate normal, invalid, and review-required cases.
lessons.takeaway: The final system is the whole path, including its failure and review routes.

lessons.title: Test, Demonstrate, and Document
lessons.objective: Verify workflow behavior and hand it off with operational notes.
lessons.concept: A project handoff includes sample payloads, expected outcomes, required credentials, test cases, known limits, recovery steps, and an explanation of how to inspect execution history.
lessons.example: Document a failed model response path and show how an operator resumes after correcting the input.
lessons.challenge: Run three acceptance tests, record evidence, fix one observed issue, and prepare a short operator guide.
lessons.takeaway: An automation is ready when another person can operate and recover it.

vibe_coding.title: Vibe Coding: Build & Ship Apps with AI
vibe_coding.description: Use AI coding assistants to prototype and ship apps while retaining control through specifications, inspection, testing, and security checks.

modules.title: What Vibe Coding Actually Means
modules.description: Use conversational coding as an iterative development technique, not a substitute for engineering judgment.
modules.story: A founder gets a working demo quickly, then discovers nobody can explain what the generated code will do with real users.
modules.discovery: Compare a fast first draft with a small change that exposes hidden assumptions and missing safeguards.

lessons.title: An Iterative Conversation with Code
lessons.objective: Describe the prompt, inspect, run, observe, and revise loop used in AI-assisted coding.
lessons.concept: Vibe coding describes building through natural-language direction and iterative AI-generated changes. The developer still owns requirements, integration, verification, and the consequences of shipping.
lessons.example: Ask an assistant for a small filter component, inspect the files changed, run it, and request one narrowly scoped revision.
lessons.challenge: Use an assistant to make one visible change in a throwaway app and record the request, changed files, and observed behavior.
lessons.takeaway: Fast generation changes the workflow; it does not transfer responsibility.

lessons.title: Where Generated Code Can Mislead
lessons.objective: Identify assumptions and risks hidden by a polished-looking prototype.
lessons.concept: A demo can omit validation, access control, error states, accessibility, and data persistence. Treat generated code as an unreviewed proposal until behavior and boundaries are checked.
lessons.example: A generated login screen may look complete but store a password in local storage or accept every credential.
lessons.challenge: Inspect a small generated interface and list three behaviors it demonstrates and three behaviors it does not prove.
lessons.takeaway: A working screen is not evidence of a safe, complete system.

modules.title: Turning Ideas into Specifications
modules.description: Convert a broad idea into user flows, acceptance criteria, boundaries, and a staged implementation plan.
modules.story: A request for a neighborhood event app sounds clear until two people disagree about who can edit an event.
modules.discovery: Find the missing decisions before asking an assistant to create files.

lessons.title: Define Users, Flows, and Acceptance Criteria
lessons.objective: Write a small specification with users, primary flows, and observable success criteria.
lessons.concept: A useful specification states who uses the feature, what they need, what is in scope, and how success can be observed. Acceptance criteria should describe behavior, not implementation guesses.
lessons.example: For event signup, define a guest's registration path, duplicate-signup behavior, confirmation, and accessible error feedback.
lessons.challenge: Turn a one-sentence app idea into three user stories and five testable acceptance criteria.
lessons.takeaway: Specific behavior gives an AI assistant something verifiable to build.

lessons.title: Bound the First Build
lessons.objective: Choose a minimum useful slice and name explicit non-goals.
lessons.concept: A small vertical slice crosses the interface and data path for one user outcome. Non-goals prevent an assistant from expanding a task into unrelated features or dependencies.
lessons.example: Build event creation and listing first; defer payments, recommendations, and social profiles.
lessons.challenge: Split a large app idea into a first vertical slice and a list of three deferred features with reasons.
lessons.takeaway: A bounded first build is easier to inspect and finish.

modules.title: Working with AI Coding Assistants
modules.description: Give assistants useful repository context and ask for bounded, reviewable changes.
modules.story: An assistant edits a project but changes styling, routing, and data handling when asked for one button.
modules.discovery: Reduce unintended work by supplying constraints and inspecting the diff after each step.

lessons.title: Provide Repository Context and Constraints
lessons.objective: Prepare a focused assistant request using relevant files, behavior, and project rules.
lessons.concept: Useful context includes the current behavior, relevant entry points, expected result, constraints, and how to verify. Share only the files needed for the change and state what must remain untouched.
lessons.example: Ask for an error message on a form, identify its component and validation function, and require existing API behavior to remain unchanged.
lessons.challenge: Write a bounded coding request for one feature and name the files and behaviors the assistant must inspect or preserve.
lessons.takeaway: Good context narrows the change and improves reviewability.

lessons.title: Review Generated Diffs
lessons.objective: Inspect a diff for scope, data flow, dependency changes, and unintended behavior.
lessons.concept: Review the complete diff, not just the final screen. Check changed files, new packages, input handling, secrets, permission boundaries, and whether the implementation matches acceptance criteria.
lessons.example: A UI request that adds a telemetry package or weakens a server check deserves review even if the button works.
lessons.challenge: Review a sample diff and classify each change as required, unrelated, risky, or needing a test.
lessons.takeaway: Generated code is a proposal that needs human review.

modules.title: Building the First Prototype
modules.description: Create a small working slice with clear data boundaries and visible behavior.
modules.story: A prototype needs to save one task and display it after a reload, not merely show a mock card.
modules.discovery: Follow one piece of data from user input through validation and persistence to the rendered result.

lessons.title: Build One Vertical Slice
lessons.objective: Implement one complete user outcome across input, processing, and display.
lessons.concept: A vertical slice connects a narrow interface to real application logic and an observable result. It reveals integration problems earlier than building every screen in isolation.
lessons.example: Submit a task title, validate it, save it through the existing data layer, and show the saved task in the list.
lessons.challenge: Use an assistant to build one end-to-end flow from your specification and verify persistence or clearly label any prototype-only storage.
lessons.takeaway: A small end-to-end path teaches more than disconnected screens.

lessons.title: Keep State and Interfaces Explicit
lessons.objective: Trace where the prototype stores state and what each interface expects.
lessons.concept: State may live in a component, URL, browser storage, or backend. Name the owner and data shape so generated changes do not silently create competing sources of truth.
lessons.example: Keep a selected filter in the URL while loading task records from one API rather than shadowing both in unrelated arrays.
lessons.challenge: Draw the state path for your prototype and add a check that confirms the UI reflects the persisted value after reload.
lessons.takeaway: Explicit state boundaries make the prototype predictable.

modules.title: Debugging AI-Generated Code
modules.description: Reproduce failures, inspect evidence, and request small corrections instead of accepting guesses.
modules.story: A generated search works for one word but returns stale results after the user changes the query.
modules.discovery: Capture the failing input and state transition before asking for a fix.

lessons.title: Reproduce and Localize a Failure
lessons.objective: Create a reliable reproduction and narrow a bug to a component or data boundary.
lessons.concept: A good bug report records expected and actual behavior, input, steps, environment, and relevant logs. Reproduction reduces speculative edits and helps distinguish cause from symptom.
lessons.example: Search for `map` then `model` quickly and observe whether the first request finishes last and overwrites the newer result.
lessons.challenge: Create a minimal failing case for a generated bug and provide the assistant with the reproduction plus the smallest relevant code area.
lessons.takeaway: Evidence first; edits second.

lessons.title: Verify the Proposed Fix
lessons.objective: Check a fix against the original failure and nearby edge cases.
lessons.concept: A plausible explanation is not proof. Rerun the exact reproduction, inspect changed code, and test adjacent cases that exercise the same boundary without broadening the task unnecessarily.
lessons.example: After fixing stale search results, test a slow response, an empty query, and a failed request.
lessons.challenge: Ask for one narrow fix, compare the diff to the diagnosis, and record results for the reproduction and two related cases.
lessons.takeaway: A fix is complete when the observed failure no longer reproduces and the change fits the cause.

modules.title: Working with Existing Codebases
modules.description: Map an unfamiliar project before changing it and follow its existing data and API contracts.
modules.story: A feature request lands in a repository with two similar components and a server route that owns the data.
modules.discovery: Locate the real render path and data source before editing the first matching filename.

lessons.title: Trace the Real Execution Path
lessons.objective: Follow an existing feature from page entry through data calls to rendering.
lessons.concept: Repository search, route definitions, imports, and call sites reveal which code actually runs. Similar old files may be unused; confirm linkage before making a change.
lessons.example: Trace a course card from API response through mapping to its click URL and detail-page request.
lessons.challenge: Document one feature's entry point, data source, transformation, render function, and action handler.
lessons.takeaway: Change the code path that executes, not the file name that looks promising.

lessons.title: Respect Contracts and Project Conventions
lessons.objective: Identify existing field names, validation, and test conventions before extending a feature.
lessons.concept: An API contract includes request shape, response shape, errors, and authorization. Reuse the established contract unless evidence shows a mismatch; translate naming at a boundary rather than changing persisted fields casually.
lessons.example: Add a display label by mapping an existing snake_case response field instead of renaming the database column.
lessons.challenge: Inspect an existing API and write down its method, fields, auth requirement, error cases, and one compatible extension point.
lessons.takeaway: Consistency reduces accidental breakage across consumers.

modules.title: Testing and Verification
modules.description: Choose checks that exercise behavior and data boundaries, not just successful rendering.
modules.story: A prototype passes a visual demo but fails when an input is empty or the network is unavailable.
modules.discovery: Write expected behavior for normal, boundary, and failure cases before calling it finished.

lessons.title: Turn Acceptance Criteria into Checks
lessons.objective: Translate user-visible requirements into repeatable verification steps.
lessons.concept: Each acceptance criterion should map to an observable check. Combine focused function tests, API checks, and manual browser paths where each is useful; do not infer behavior from syntax alone.
lessons.example: For signup, verify valid input, missing email, duplicate email, and a failed server response.
lessons.challenge: Create a verification table for your prototype with criterion, setup, action, expected result, and actual result.
lessons.takeaway: Verification should match the requirements that motivated the change.

lessons.title: Check Boundaries and Failure Paths
lessons.objective: Test malformed input, denied access, empty results, and dependency failures.
lessons.concept: Boundary checks reveal whether the system rejects invalid data, handles unavailable services, and avoids exposing private information. Use a safe test environment and non-production data.
lessons.example: Submit an unknown record ID and confirm the API returns a client error rather than an unhandled database exception.
lessons.challenge: Test three failure paths in your prototype and record both the user-facing response and the server-side evidence.
lessons.takeaway: Failure behavior is part of the feature contract.

modules.title: Shipping the Application
modules.description: Prepare a safe, understandable release with configuration, version control, and rollback awareness.
modules.story: A demo is ready, but its API key is committed and nobody knows how to undo the deployment.
modules.discovery: Review the release as an operator who must configure, observe, and recover it.

lessons.title: Version Control and Release Preparation
lessons.objective: Use a focused commit and a release checklist to make changes traceable.
lessons.concept: Version control records reviewable changes and supports rollback. A release checklist covers configuration, secrets, data migrations, tests, build output, and the owner responsible for monitoring.
lessons.example: Review a branch diff, remove a local credential, run checks, and commit only the files that implement the feature.
lessons.challenge: Prepare a release checklist for your app and identify which settings must be configured outside source control.
lessons.takeaway: Shipping is a controlled handoff, not just uploading files.

lessons.title: Security and Post-Release Checks
lessons.objective: Review common security boundaries and verify the deployed behavior after release.
lessons.concept: Do not trust client input, expose secrets, or rely on hidden UI for authorization. After release, check health, key user flows, logs, and a recovery path using non-sensitive test data.
lessons.example: A hidden admin button is not access control; the server must verify permission before returning protected data.
lessons.challenge: Run a post-release checklist that tests one allowed action, one denied action, configuration, and rollback instructions.
lessons.takeaway: A release is not complete until its real environment is checked.

modules.title: Build Challenge: Specify, Build, Inspect, Ship
modules.description: Deliver a small application feature with a specification, reviewed AI changes, verification, and a release note.
modules.story: You have one day to build a useful internal tool without hiding unfinished behavior behind a polished mockup.
modules.discovery: Show how a requirement becomes a tested and reviewable increment.

lessons.title: Implement the Build Challenge
lessons.objective: Build a bounded user workflow and preserve evidence of what the assistant changed.
lessons.concept: The challenge combines specification, a vertical slice, diff review, and targeted tests. Keep the first release small enough that you can explain the data path and major failure behavior.
lessons.example: Build a team handoff board that creates a task, validates its owner, and shows saved tasks after reload.
lessons.challenge: Ship your chosen slice with acceptance criteria, inspected diffs, and checks for one normal and two failure cases.
lessons.takeaway: Build with AI, but understand the result well enough to maintain it.

lessons.title: Present the Evidence and Next Steps
lessons.objective: Explain what works, what was verified, known limits, and the next safe increment.
lessons.concept: A useful demo distinguishes implemented behavior from planned work. Show the acceptance criteria, evidence, known risks, and how to reproduce the main flow.
lessons.example: Demonstrate the task flow, a validation error, and a test result before listing deferred notifications as future work.
lessons.challenge: Record a short demo or walkthrough with one successful path, one failure path, and a concise handoff note.
lessons.takeaway: Clear limits make a prototype more trustworthy.

generative_ai_llm.title: Generative AI & LLM Application Development
generative_ai_llm.description: Build LLM applications using model APIs, structured outputs, embeddings, conversation state, and practical reliability controls.

modules.title: Generative AI Foundations
modules.description: Understand generative systems, model behavior, and the difference between generation and retrieval.
modules.story: A team asks a model for an answer about a document it has never seen and mistakes a confident guess for a source-backed fact.
modules.discovery: Separate what the model can generate from what the application must retrieve or verify.

lessons.title: Generation, Training, and Inference
lessons.objective: Distinguish training from inference and describe the role of learned parameters.
lessons.concept: Generative models learn statistical patterns during training and use those patterns to produce outputs during inference. The deployed model does not automatically know private or newly created application data.
lessons.example: A model can explain a general programming term but cannot know your team's latest runbook unless you provide or retrieve it.
lessons.challenge: Classify five example tasks as general generation, private-data lookup, or a combination, and explain what application support each needs.
lessons.takeaway: Generation is a capability; current private knowledge must come from an explicit source.

lessons.title: Model Limits and Application Boundaries
lessons.objective: Identify where an application needs retrieval, validation, or a human decision.
lessons.concept: Models may produce unsupported details, miss instructions, or vary across runs. Application design should constrain inputs and outputs and assign deterministic decisions to ordinary code where possible.
lessons.example: Use code to enforce a refund limit while a model drafts a polite explanation grounded in approved policy text.
lessons.challenge: Mark the model and deterministic boundaries in a support assistant flow and justify each boundary.
lessons.takeaway: Use a model for language tasks without making it the authority for every decision.

modules.title: LLMs and Context
modules.description: Manage context, message roles, token limits, and conversation inputs in an application.
modules.story: A chat feature forgets an earlier preference after a long conversation and includes irrelevant history in each call.
modules.discovery: Find which context is necessary for the current response and which state should be stored separately.

lessons.title: Messages, Roles, and Context Windows
lessons.objective: Construct a model request with distinct instructions, user input, and relevant context.
lessons.concept: Chat APIs commonly represent instructions and turns as structured messages. Context windows bound the total prompt and response; role boundaries help organize intent but do not replace security checks.
lessons.example: Send stable system guidance, a short user question, and one retrieved policy excerpt as distinct messages.
lessons.challenge: Prepare a request with explicit roles and trim irrelevant conversation turns while retaining the facts needed to answer.
lessons.takeaway: Context is a limited input budget that should be managed intentionally.

lessons.title: Conversation State and Summaries
lessons.objective: Choose which conversation facts to retain and how to refresh a bounded summary.
lessons.concept: Conversation history is not durable application memory by itself. Store only needed, permission-appropriate facts and refresh summaries with references to their source when decisions depend on them.
lessons.example: Keep a user's chosen language as explicit session state while summarizing an older troubleshooting exchange.
lessons.challenge: Design a conversation state record with an expiry policy and show which details should not be retained.
lessons.takeaway: Memory is an application design choice, not an automatic model property.

modules.title: APIs and Model Interaction
modules.description: Call model APIs with controlled inputs, timeouts, error handling, and traceable settings.
modules.story: A user-facing feature stalls when a provider is slow and logs an entire prompt containing personal data.
modules.discovery: Inspect request settings, response metadata, and logs as part of the application boundary.

lessons.title: Make a Model API Request
lessons.objective: Send a minimal model request and capture the response and relevant usage metadata.
lessons.concept: An API request includes model choice, messages, generation settings, and optional output constraints. Keep provider credentials on the server and avoid logging sensitive prompt content by default.
lessons.example: A server endpoint accepts a short question, adds approved instructions, calls the provider, and returns the answer with a request ID.
lessons.challenge: Sketch or build a server-side model call with a timeout, request ID, and a redacted error response.
lessons.takeaway: Treat the provider as an external dependency with a defined contract.

lessons.title: Latency, Errors, and Usage
lessons.objective: Handle provider failures and observe latency and token usage without exposing secrets.
lessons.concept: Rate limits, network errors, timeouts, and provider changes are normal failure cases. Track request IDs, latency, and usage totals so the application can diagnose cost and reliability.
lessons.example: Return a retryable service-unavailable response after a timeout while keeping the provider key and raw exception private.
lessons.challenge: Create a failure table for timeout, rate limit, and invalid request; specify response, retry policy, and safe telemetry for each.
lessons.takeaway: Operational behavior belongs in the model integration design.

modules.title: Structured Outputs
modules.description: Request, parse, and validate machine-readable model responses.
modules.story: An application expects a JSON action plan but receives extra commentary and a missing required field.
modules.discovery: Decide what can be guaranteed by the API schema and what the application still must validate.

lessons.title: Constrain Output Shape
lessons.objective: Define a compact output schema that matches the application's next step.
lessons.concept: Structured-output modes can constrain syntax, but semantic checks remain necessary. Specify required fields, types, allowed values, and length limits around the actual downstream contract.
lessons.example: Require a summary string, an array of evidence IDs, and a category from a fixed enum.
lessons.challenge: Define a JSON schema for a document summary and add one invalid example for each required field.
lessons.takeaway: A schema narrows output; validation decides whether it is usable.

lessons.title: Parse, Validate, and Recover
lessons.objective: Reject malformed or unsupported fields and provide a recoverable user path.
lessons.concept: Parse responses as untrusted data. Validate structure and business rules, handle refusal or truncation explicitly, and avoid blindly retrying a response that failed for a permanent reason.
lessons.example: A generated date is parsed and checked against a permitted date range before being saved.
lessons.challenge: Write validation cases for a missing key, unexpected enum, oversized text, and provider refusal; define safe handling for each.
lessons.takeaway: Only validated output should enter application state.

modules.title: Embeddings
modules.description: Represent text for semantic comparison and understand the limits of vector similarity.
modules.story: A search box misses a useful article because it uses different words from the user's question.
modules.discovery: Compare literal keyword overlap with similarity based on meaning-bearing vector representations.

lessons.title: From Text to Embeddings
lessons.objective: Explain how an embedding maps text to a vector used for similarity comparisons.
lessons.concept: An embedding model maps text into a numeric vector space where related items may be nearby. Similarity is a retrieval signal, not a guarantee that two passages answer the same question.
lessons.example: Compare embeddings for “reset an account password” and “recover login access,” then inspect whether their source passages are actually relevant.
lessons.challenge: Choose five query-document pairs and label which semantic matches are useful and which are misleading.
lessons.takeaway: Vector closeness helps find candidates; the application still judges relevance.

lessons.title: Similarity Search and Metadata
lessons.objective: Combine vector candidates with metadata filters and inspect retrieval results.
lessons.concept: A vector index returns approximate neighbors. Metadata filters can scope by tenant, date, or document type, while result inspection checks whether the candidate set is relevant and authorized.
lessons.example: Search policy embeddings only within the caller's organization and the current policy version.
lessons.challenge: Design a retrieval query with a semantic term and two metadata filters; list a test that catches cross-tenant leakage.
lessons.takeaway: Retrieval quality and access boundaries must be designed together.

modules.title: Building an LLM Application
modules.description: Connect a focused user task to validated model behavior and a maintainable service boundary.
modules.story: A prototype turns a user request into a draft report, but users need to know which inputs shaped it.
modules.discovery: Trace input, model request, response validation, and output display as a single application flow.

lessons.title: Design the User-to-Model Path
lessons.objective: Map user input through server validation, model invocation, and response rendering.
lessons.concept: A reliable application defines the user task, permitted input, server-side instruction, provider boundary, validation, and user-visible failure states. Avoid calling providers directly from a browser with secret credentials.
lessons.example: A server receives a report topic, verifies access to its source data, generates a draft, and returns a request ID for feedback.
lessons.challenge: Draw your app's data flow and identify where authorization, validation, logging, and error handling occur.
lessons.takeaway: The model call is one component in a larger application path.

lessons.title: Add Feedback and Fallbacks
lessons.objective: Give users a useful fallback and a way to report or correct a generated result.
lessons.concept: Fallbacks may offer retry, manual completion, or a clear unavailable state. Feedback should capture useful quality signals without collecting unnecessary sensitive content.
lessons.example: If a draft fails validation, let the user edit a blank template instead of displaying an unverified response.
lessons.challenge: Specify three failure states and the user action available in each; include a minimal feedback event for a poor answer.
lessons.takeaway: A robust app remains usable when generation fails.

modules.title: Conversation and Memory
modules.description: Implement conversation continuity with explicit state, privacy limits, and user control.
modules.story: A user expects an assistant to remember a chosen format but not retain a private one-time disclosure forever.
modules.discovery: Separate short-lived conversational context from durable preferences and records.

lessons.title: Keep Useful Conversation Context
lessons.objective: Summarize or select prior turns that are relevant to the current task.
lessons.concept: Long histories consume tokens and can bury important constraints. A summary should preserve decisions and open questions, be refreshed as the conversation changes, and avoid turning guesses into stored facts.
lessons.example: Retain the confirmed project language and unresolved deployment question, but omit unrelated small talk.
lessons.challenge: Reduce a sample chat to a context note with confirmed facts, source turns, and unresolved items.
lessons.takeaway: Carry forward relevant context with provenance.

lessons.title: Memory, Retention, and User Control
lessons.objective: Define what the application stores, how long it stays, and how a user can correct or remove it.
lessons.concept: Persistent memory is database state subject to access, retention, and deletion rules. Store the minimum needed, distinguish user-provided facts from model-generated inferences, and expose a correction path.
lessons.example: Store a user-selected response style with an update and delete control, not a hidden psychological profile inferred from chats.
lessons.challenge: Write a memory policy for one feature with stored fields, purpose, expiry, access, correction, and deletion behavior.
lessons.takeaway: Memory should be transparent and bounded.

modules.title: Reliability, Cost, and Safety
modules.description: Control model spend and failure impact with limits, validation, and privacy-aware design.
modules.story: A popular feature experiences a cost spike after repeated long requests and unbounded output generation.
modules.discovery: Find which product choices determine call volume, input size, output size, and risk.

lessons.title: Bound Latency and Cost
lessons.objective: Estimate cost drivers and set practical limits for model inputs and outputs.
lessons.concept: Usage depends on request volume, input and output tokens, model pricing, retries, and caching behavior. Establish limits and monitor actual usage before optimizing based on assumptions.
lessons.example: Limit a summary input to relevant passages and cap output length; measure latency and usage on representative requests.
lessons.challenge: Estimate monthly usage for a feature under low and high traffic and name two controls for an unexpected spike.
lessons.takeaway: Cost and latency are product constraints that can be measured.

lessons.title: Privacy and Safe Failure
lessons.objective: Minimize sensitive data sent to models and prevent unsafe output from becoming an action.
lessons.concept: Classify input data, remove fields not needed for the task, enforce access on the server, and keep generated text separate from executable actions until checked or approved.
lessons.example: Redact account numbers before summarization and require a person to approve a generated account change.
lessons.challenge: Review a proposed prompt for sensitive data and side effects; rewrite it to minimize exposure and add an approval boundary.
lessons.takeaway: Limit what the model sees and what its output can do.

modules.title: LLM Application Project
modules.description: Build and evaluate a small LLM application with an explicit contract, data flow, and recovery behavior.
modules.story: A learner builds a focused assistant that helps answer one recurring question from approved material.
modules.discovery: Demonstrate the full behavior on a typical query and a case the app should decline or route for review.

lessons.title: Build the Application Slice
lessons.objective: Implement one end-to-end LLM feature with validated input and output.
lessons.concept: The project combines model API use, bounded context, structured or clearly formatted results, validation, user feedback, and safe failure handling.
lessons.example: Build an assistant that drafts a response from a supplied policy excerpt and returns the supporting excerpt with the draft.
lessons.challenge: Deliver your app slice with a normal case, missing-context case, and provider-failure behavior.
lessons.takeaway: A useful LLM app is a controlled workflow around generation.

lessons.title: Evaluate and Present the Project
lessons.objective: Present behavior, limitations, and evidence from a small repeatable evaluation set.
lessons.concept: A project review should show inputs, expected criteria, actual outputs, failures found, and changes made. Separate known behavior from future work and report which cases were not tested.
lessons.example: Compare five representative prompts using the same factual-support rubric before and after a prompt change.
lessons.challenge: Run a five-case check, write a concise results note, and demonstrate one limitation honestly.
lessons.takeaway: Evidence and limits make an AI project easier to trust and improve.

rag_knowledge_systems.title: RAG & Knowledge Systems
rag_knowledge_systems.description: Build grounded knowledge assistants with document ingestion, chunking, retrieval, citations, and evaluation.

modules.title: Why LLMs Need External Knowledge
modules.description: Understand what retrieval adds and define source, freshness, and permission boundaries.
modules.story: A policy assistant gives an outdated answer because its model was not trained on the latest internal policy.
modules.discovery: Trace the difference between a model's general language capability and the application's current source material.

lessons.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation in a System
lessons.objective: Explain how retrieval supplies relevant external text to a generation step.
lessons.concept: RAG retrieves candidate source passages for a query and provides them as context to a model. It can improve grounding in a chosen corpus, but it does not guarantee correct retrieval or faithful answers.
lessons.example: Search an approved travel policy, provide the relevant section to a model, and ask for a short answer with a citation.
lessons.challenge: Draw an input-query-retrieval-generation flow and label what each stage can fail to do.
lessons.takeaway: RAG connects a model to sources; retrieval quality remains a separate problem.

lessons.title: Knowledge Boundaries and Access
lessons.objective: Define which documents an assistant can retrieve for each user and task.
lessons.concept: A knowledge system needs source ownership, freshness, permissions, and deletion behavior. Authorization must constrain retrieval before passages are sent to the model.
lessons.example: Filter employee handbook documents by organization and access group before semantic search.
lessons.challenge: Create an access matrix for three document groups and verify that each test user retrieves only permitted sources.
lessons.takeaway: A relevant passage is not appropriate if the caller is not allowed to see it.

modules.title: Embeddings and Semantic Search
modules.description: Create embeddings, retrieve candidates, and combine similarity with metadata and permission filters.
modules.story: A question about “parental leave” should find a policy section titled “family care absence.”
modules.discovery: Test whether semantically related wording retrieves the intended source rather than just a nearby topic.

lessons.title: Embed and Index Text
lessons.objective: Describe the process of embedding document passages and storing vectors with metadata.
lessons.concept: An embedding is a numeric representation used for nearest-neighbor search. Store the source ID, passage boundaries, version, and access metadata alongside each vector so results can be traced and filtered.
lessons.example: Index a policy section with document ID, heading path, version date, and permission group.
lessons.challenge: Design the fields for one indexed passage and explain how a source update would invalidate or replace it.
lessons.takeaway: Vectors need source metadata to become usable knowledge records.

lessons.title: Retrieve and Inspect Candidates
lessons.objective: Measure whether top retrieved passages are relevant to a query.
lessons.concept: Semantic search returns candidates, often ranked by similarity. Inspect top-k results across paraphrases and ambiguous questions; add keyword or metadata filters where vector similarity alone is insufficient.
lessons.example: Compare retrieval for “expense reimbursement” and “how do I get paid back?” and inspect their source headings.
lessons.challenge: Build a ten-query retrieval set and mark each top result relevant, partially relevant, or misleading.
lessons.takeaway: A similarity score is a ranking aid, not a relevance verdict.

modules.title: Document Ingestion
modules.description: Turn source documents into versioned, traceable text records suitable for retrieval.
modules.story: A team imports PDFs, HTML pages, and office documents but loses headings and document dates.
modules.discovery: Inspect what information survives extraction and decide how to detect incomplete or stale documents.

lessons.title: Extract and Normalize Documents
lessons.objective: Design a repeatable extraction step that preserves useful structure and source identity.
lessons.concept: Ingestion converts files or pages into text and metadata. Preserve headings, page or section references, source IDs, language, and timestamps; flag empty or low-quality extraction for review.
lessons.example: Extract a PDF handbook into section records with its page number and title hierarchy.
lessons.challenge: Create an ingestion checklist for two source formats and specify how malformed text is detected.
lessons.takeaway: Retrieval quality begins with faithful, traceable ingestion.

lessons.title: Versioning and Updating a Corpus
lessons.objective: Handle source changes without leaving stale or duplicate passages searchable.
lessons.concept: A corpus update needs a stable document identity, version or checksum, active status, and a replacement strategy. Deletions and permission changes must propagate to indexed chunks.
lessons.example: When a policy revision arrives, mark the previous version inactive and index the new version before publishing it.
lessons.challenge: Describe a safe re-index plan for an updated document and test that only the current approved version appears in search.
lessons.takeaway: Keep the index aligned with its authoritative source.

modules.title: Chunking and Retrieval
modules.description: Choose passage boundaries and retrieval settings that preserve enough context for useful answers.
modules.story: Search retrieves one sentence without its exception clause, causing an answer to overstate a policy.
modules.discovery: Compare fixed-size chunks with structure-aware chunks around headings and complete ideas.

lessons.title: Choose Chunk Boundaries
lessons.objective: Select chunk boundaries that retain a coherent passage and its source location.
lessons.concept: Chunks that are too small lose context; chunks that are too large dilute retrieval. Use document structure where possible, keep useful overlap modest, and retain exact source offsets or headings.
lessons.example: Keep a policy rule and its exception together under one section heading rather than splitting them across unrelated windows.
lessons.challenge: Chunk a short guide in two ways and compare whether each chunk preserves the rule, exception, and heading.
lessons.takeaway: A chunk should be small enough to retrieve and complete enough to interpret.

lessons.title: Tune Retrieval for a Query
lessons.objective: Combine query preparation, top-k selection, and filters for a defined search task.
lessons.concept: Retrieval settings depend on the corpus and query. Top-k, thresholding, metadata filters, hybrid search, and reranking change the candidate set and must be evaluated together.
lessons.example: Filter a product manual by product version, retrieve candidate sections, and rerank them against the full question.
lessons.challenge: Tune a small set of retrieval options against five queries and document where precision or coverage changes.
lessons.takeaway: Tune retrieval against observed queries, not intuition alone.

modules.title: Building a RAG Pipeline
modules.description: Connect ingestion, retrieval, prompt context, generation, and source-aware response handling.
modules.story: A prototype retrieves passages but the final answer adds instructions that were never in the documents.
modules.discovery: Follow evidence through the pipeline and identify where generated claims can drift from it.

lessons.title: Assemble Retrieval and Generation
lessons.objective: Build a pipeline that supplies selected passages and a clear answer task to a model.
lessons.concept: A RAG pipeline embeds or searches a query, selects passages, formats bounded context, asks for an answer, and validates the response. Keep retrieved material distinct from instructions and user text.
lessons.example: Retrieve two approved setup-guide sections and ask the model to answer only from them, returning “not found” when evidence is absent.
lessons.challenge: Build a small pipeline and test a supported question plus one question not covered by its documents.
lessons.takeaway: A grounded answer depends on each pipeline stage preserving the source boundary.

lessons.title: Prompt with Retrieved Context
lessons.objective: Instruct a model to use retrieved evidence and signal when evidence is insufficient.
lessons.concept: The prompt should delimit source passages, explain the task, request citations, and state how to handle conflicts or missing evidence. Retrieved text itself must be treated as data, not trusted instructions.
lessons.example: Wrap policy excerpts with source labels and ask for a concise answer plus the source label supporting each factual statement.
lessons.challenge: Write a context prompt and test it against relevant evidence, conflicting passages, and no retrieved evidence.
lessons.takeaway: Context instructions help, but application checks still matter.

modules.title: Retrieval Quality
modules.description: Diagnose missed, irrelevant, stale, and unauthorized retrieval results.
modules.story: A knowledge assistant gives one accurate answer and misses a critical exception in the next query.
modules.discovery: Measure retrieval independently from answer fluency so a polished response cannot hide poor search.

lessons.title: Build a Retrieval Test Set
lessons.objective: Create query-to-source examples and measure whether retrieval returns the expected passages.
lessons.concept: A retrieval set records questions, relevant source IDs, acceptable alternatives, and permission context. Recall and precision trade off; inspect failures by query type before changing parameters.
lessons.example: For each policy question, note the section that answers it and any exception that must also be retrieved.
lessons.challenge: Create eight retrieval cases, run the current search, and classify each failure as extraction, chunking, query, filter, or ranking.
lessons.takeaway: Test retrieval as its own system component.

lessons.title: Improve Retrieval Without Hiding Failures
lessons.objective: Choose a targeted retrieval change and verify it against the full test set.
lessons.concept: Changes to chunking, metadata, hybrid search, thresholds, or reranking can improve some queries and harm others. Keep a baseline and rerun all cases after each controlled change.
lessons.example: Add a heading-based filter for product version and check both version-specific and general queries.
lessons.challenge: Make one retrieval change, compare before-and-after results, and document regressions as well as gains.
lessons.takeaway: A targeted improvement must preserve previously working cases.

modules.title: Citations and Grounding
modules.description: Return source references and check whether answer claims are actually supported by retrieved material.
modules.story: A user clicks a citation that points to the right document but the wrong paragraph.
modules.discovery: Trace every displayed source link back to the exact passage used in the response.

lessons.title: Attach Traceable Citations
lessons.objective: Represent citations with stable source identifiers and useful passage locations.
lessons.concept: A citation needs enough identity to retrieve the original source and location, such as document ID, version, heading, page, or offset. Links should resolve to an authorized source view.
lessons.example: Return a policy name, revision date, and section anchor rather than a generic link to a document home page.
lessons.challenge: Add source metadata to a response structure and verify that each citation opens the cited current passage.
lessons.takeaway: A citation is useful only when it is accurate and traceable.

lessons.title: Check Claim-to-Evidence Support
lessons.objective: Review whether each answer claim is entailed or qualified by its cited passage.
lessons.concept: Retrieved passages may be related but fail to support a claim. Separate claims, compare each with its evidence, preserve qualifications, and mark unsupported statements rather than smoothing over gaps.
lessons.example: A passage says “some requests take five days”; the answer must not state “all requests take five days.”
lessons.challenge: Break a sample answer into claims, match each to evidence, and rewrite unsupported or overgeneralized claims.
lessons.takeaway: Grounding means support, not just topical similarity.

modules.title: RAG Evaluation
modules.description: Evaluate retrieval, answer quality, grounding, and failure handling with repeatable cases.
modules.story: A release improves answer style while silently lowering the rate of correct citations.
modules.discovery: Score retrieval and generated answers separately, then compare their relationship.

lessons.title: Evaluate Retrieval and Answers Separately
lessons.objective: Choose distinct measures for finding evidence and using evidence in a response.
lessons.concept: Retrieval evaluation checks whether relevant passages are found. Answer evaluation checks factual support, completeness, citation quality, and abstention behavior; one aggregate score can hide different failures.
lessons.example: Use a known source set to score retrieval recall, then review whether generated answers preserve the source's exception.
lessons.challenge: Build a two-part rubric for ten cases and report retrieval errors separately from generation errors.
lessons.takeaway: Separate stages to locate the source of quality loss.

lessons.title: Regression and Adversarial Cases
lessons.objective: Test corpus changes and misleading inputs without losing known behavior.
lessons.concept: A regression set should include common questions, edge cases, stale versions, conflicting sources, and attempts to treat document text as instructions. Re-run it when prompts, models, or indexes change.
lessons.example: Include a passage that says “ignore prior directions” and ensure it is treated as quoted document content.
lessons.challenge: Add three adversarial or conflict cases to your suite and define expected safe behavior for each.
lessons.takeaway: Test what should happen when evidence is confusing or hostile.

modules.title: Build a Knowledge Assistant
modules.description: Deliver a source-grounded assistant with access controls, citations, and an evaluation record.
modules.story: A small team needs answers from a bounded handbook and must be able to inspect every source.
modules.discovery: Demonstrate normal answers, missing evidence, and a permission boundary.

lessons.title: Build the Knowledge Assistant
lessons.objective: Connect a small corpus to retrieval, generation, citations, and safe access filtering.
lessons.concept: The capstone combines document ingestion, chunk metadata, permission-aware retrieval, bounded generation, citations, and visible behavior for no-answer cases.
lessons.example: Answer a handbook question with a section link, and decline to answer when the corpus has no supporting passage.
lessons.challenge: Build the assistant on a small approved corpus and verify supported, unsupported, and unauthorized queries.
lessons.takeaway: Grounded systems expose their sources and their boundaries.

lessons.title: Review Quality and Handoff
lessons.objective: Present evaluation evidence and document how the corpus and assistant should be maintained.
lessons.concept: A handoff explains source ownership, re-indexing, access updates, known limits, test cases, and where to inspect failures. Report measured behavior rather than promising perfect accuracy.
lessons.example: Show retrieval misses and citation mismatches from your evaluation set alongside the fixes you applied.
lessons.challenge: Write an operator note with corpus update steps, a five-case evaluation summary, and one known limitation.
lessons.takeaway: A knowledge assistant remains reliable only when its sources and tests are maintained.

ai_agents.title: AI Agents & Tool Use
ai_agents.description: Design bounded agent loops that use tools, manage state, and recover safely from errors.

modules.title: From Chatbots to Agents
modules.description: Distinguish a conversational response from a system that selects and executes actions.
modules.story: A travel assistant can describe a flight, but users now ask it to check dates and prepare a booking.
modules.discovery: Identify the additional state, tools, and safeguards that turn a response into an action loop.

lessons.title: Agent, Tool, and Environment
lessons.objective: Describe an agent as a model-driven loop interacting with tools and an environment.
lessons.concept: An agent system repeatedly observes context, selects an allowed action, receives a result, and decides whether to continue. The model is only one component; application code enforces the available action boundary.
lessons.example: A calendar assistant can inspect free/busy data, propose a slot, and wait for confirmation before creating an event.
lessons.challenge: Diagram a simple agent with input, two tools, observations, stop conditions, and one action requiring approval.
lessons.takeaway: An agent is a controlled system around a model, not a model with unlimited authority.

lessons.title: Choose When an Agent Is Appropriate
lessons.objective: Compare an agent loop with a fixed workflow for a bounded task.
lessons.concept: Agents help when the next useful step depends on observations that are not known in advance. Fixed workflows are often simpler and more predictable when the steps are stable.
lessons.example: Use a fixed workflow for monthly report generation but an agent loop to investigate varied support questions using approved read-only tools.
lessons.challenge: Evaluate three tasks and choose fixed workflow or agent for each, citing uncertainty, cost, and impact.
lessons.takeaway: Use an agent only when adaptive action provides real value.

modules.title: Tools and Function Calling
modules.description: Define narrow tool contracts and validate every proposed call and argument.
modules.story: An assistant is given a powerful generic database tool when it only needs to look up a shipping status.
modules.discovery: Reduce tool capability until each operation has an explicit purpose and permission boundary.

lessons.title: Design a Tool Contract
lessons.objective: Specify a tool's name, purpose, typed inputs, output, and failure behavior.
lessons.concept: A tool contract should be narrow, typed, and documented. Separate read and write actions, reject unknown arguments, and return bounded results that do not leak unrelated records.
lessons.example: Provide `get_order_status(order_id)` rather than a generic SQL execution tool.
lessons.challenge: Write a contract for one read-only tool with required fields, validation rules, and two possible errors.
lessons.takeaway: Tool design defines what an agent is able to do.

lessons.title: Validate Function Calls
lessons.objective: Check model-proposed tool names and arguments before execution.
lessons.concept: Function calling produces a structured proposal, not an authorization decision. Validate schema, user permissions, resource ownership, and business rules in trusted application code before invoking a tool.
lessons.example: Reject an order lookup if the authenticated user does not own that order, even when the model supplied a valid UUID.
lessons.challenge: Test valid, malformed, unknown-tool, and unauthorized calls against a tool dispatcher.
lessons.takeaway: A valid function-call shape does not mean the action is permitted.

modules.title: Agent Loops
modules.description: Implement a bounded observe-act loop with explicit stop conditions and traceable steps.
modules.story: A research agent keeps searching after it already has enough evidence and uses its entire time budget.
modules.discovery: Make continuation depend on explicit progress, limits, and a clear completion condition.

lessons.title: Observe, Act, and Continue
lessons.objective: Trace observations and tool results through a multi-step agent loop.
lessons.concept: Each loop step should record the model decision, validated action, tool result, and updated context. This makes the loop inspectable and lets the application detect repeated or unproductive actions.
lessons.example: Search an approved knowledge base, inspect two passages, and stop when the requested answer has sufficient cited evidence.
lessons.challenge: Trace a three-step tool sequence and mark what new observation justifies each next action.
lessons.takeaway: Every next step should be grounded in a new observation or a defined plan.

lessons.title: Set Budgets and Stop Conditions
lessons.objective: Bound steps, time, tool calls, and output size for an agent execution.
lessons.concept: A loop needs maximum iterations, timeouts, per-tool limits, and clear success or failure stop conditions. Reaching a budget should produce a safe partial result or handoff, not silent unbounded work.
lessons.example: Allow at most four read-only searches and stop with a review request if no source supports an answer.
lessons.challenge: Define budgets and stop behavior for a five-minute research task, including what the user sees when the budget is reached.
lessons.takeaway: A bounded loop is easier to operate and safer to recover.

modules.title: Planning and Task Decomposition
modules.description: Turn user goals into small, observable subgoals without trusting hidden plans as facts.
modules.story: A user asks for a comparison report, and an agent must gather evidence from several approved sources.
modules.discovery: Check that every planned subgoal contributes to the requested outcome and has a way to verify completion.

lessons.title: Create an Inspectable Plan
lessons.objective: Break a request into subgoals with evidence and completion criteria.
lessons.concept: A plan is a working proposal. Keep steps small, identify required inputs and tools, and revise it when observations contradict assumptions; do not present internal reasoning as a verified result.
lessons.example: Compare three products by gathering current price, warranty, and availability from approved sources.
lessons.challenge: Write a four-step plan with one evidence requirement and one completion check per step.
lessons.takeaway: Plans organize work; evidence confirms progress.

lessons.title: Recover from Missing or Conflicting Evidence
lessons.objective: Pause or revise a plan when required information is unavailable or inconsistent.
lessons.concept: When sources conflict, tools fail, or a subgoal cannot be completed, an agent should surface the gap, seek an allowed alternative, or ask a person rather than inventing a resolution.
lessons.example: Two product pages list different warranty periods; preserve both source dates and ask for review.
lessons.challenge: Add a conflict branch to your plan and specify the exact evidence that triggers clarification instead of continuing.
lessons.takeaway: A missing fact is a useful result when it prevents a false conclusion.

modules.title: Memory and State
modules.description: Separate transient reasoning context from durable, permissioned application state.
modules.story: An assistant remembers a task ID during one run but accidentally carries it into another user's session.
modules.discovery: Trace which state belongs to a single execution, a user, or a shared system.

lessons.title: Execution State and Checkpoints
lessons.objective: Store the minimum state needed to resume a multi-step run safely.
lessons.concept: Execution state can include the request ID, completed steps, observations, and pending approvals. Persist stable identifiers and checkpoints; avoid storing raw sensitive context without a clear need and retention rule.
lessons.example: Save a research run's source IDs and completed comparisons so a timeout can resume without repeating external actions.
