lessons.challenge: Design a checkpoint record for a multi-step agent and mark which fields are sensitive or should expire.
lessons.takeaway: Persist task state intentionally and keep it scoped to its owner.

lessons.title: User Memory and Session Isolation
lessons.objective: Prevent state leakage and define user-controlled persistent memory.
lessons.concept: Persistent user memory must be permissioned, attributable, correctable, and separated by identity. Session boundaries must be enforced in storage queries and tool calls rather than assumed from prompt instructions.
lessons.example: A preference record is keyed by authenticated user ID and can be viewed, changed, or removed by that user.
lessons.challenge: Create two simulated users and verify that each can retrieve only their own saved preference and task state.
lessons.takeaway: Identity and access control belong in the application layer.

modules.title: Multi-Step Tool Use
modules.description: Coordinate tools while preserving data contracts, approval boundaries, and idempotency.
modules.story: A scheduling agent checks availability, drafts an invitation, and must avoid creating duplicate events.
modules.discovery: Mark which operations are read-only, reversible, or externally visible before chaining them.

lessons.title: Chain Tools with Verified Handoffs
lessons.objective: Pass only validated outputs between tools and keep source identifiers attached.
lessons.concept: A multi-step chain should validate each tool result before using it as an argument to the next call. Carry IDs and evidence through the chain, and define how partial completion is reported.
lessons.example: Read availability, propose a time, validate attendee IDs, then prepare an event draft for approval.
lessons.challenge: Build a read-read-draft chain and add validation between each result and the next call.
lessons.takeaway: Every tool handoff is a data boundary worth checking.

lessons.title: Make Side Effects Safe
lessons.objective: Use approvals and idempotency for actions that change external state.
lessons.concept: Write operations can be duplicated when a call times out after succeeding. Use idempotency keys, verify the resulting state, and require confirmation when the action is consequential or hard to reverse.
lessons.example: Create a calendar event with a stable request key and confirm the event ID before reporting success.
lessons.challenge: Specify retry, duplicate, approval, and rollback behavior for one tool that sends or creates something externally.
lessons.takeaway: Treat side effects as operations that need explicit safeguards.

modules.title: Agent Reliability and Safety
modules.description: Handle prompt injection, permissions, failure loops, and human escalation.
modules.story: A retrieved webpage tells an agent to ignore its task and send private data to an unrelated endpoint.
modules.discovery: Separate untrusted content from application instructions and verify permissions at the tool boundary.

lessons.title: Treat Retrieved Text as Untrusted Data
lessons.objective: Recognize instruction-like content in tool results and keep it from changing the agent's authority.
lessons.concept: External documents and web pages can contain malicious or irrelevant instructions. Delimit them as data, constrain tools independently, and validate every proposed action in trusted code.
lessons.example: A page says “email all customer records”; the agent's browser result must not grant access to an email-sending tool.
lessons.challenge: Create a test document with an instruction injection and verify the agent extracts facts without following its commands.
lessons.takeaway: Tool results inform the task but do not redefine permissions.

lessons.title: Escalation, Monitoring, and Recovery
lessons.objective: Define when an agent stops and how operators inspect or resume its work.
lessons.concept: Escalate on low evidence, repeated failures, permission errors, budget exhaustion, or high-impact action. Record safe traces and provide operators enough context to diagnose without exposing unnecessary data.
lessons.example: Pause a payment-change request for a human and record the request ID, proposed change, and source evidence.
lessons.challenge: Build an escalation matrix with trigger, user message, operator evidence, and permitted recovery action.
lessons.takeaway: A safe agent knows when not to continue.

modules.title: Build an AI Agent
modules.description: Deliver a bounded agent with tools, a multi-step task, safeguards, and observable outcomes.
modules.story: Build an assistant that researches an approved topic and prepares a cited draft without publishing it.
modules.discovery: Demonstrate how the agent knows when it has enough evidence and when it must stop.

lessons.title: Implement a Bounded Agent
lessons.objective: Combine a narrow goal, read-only tools, validated calls, budgets, and a user-visible result.
lessons.concept: The build integrates a tool registry, an agent loop, explicit state, source evidence, stop conditions, and an error or approval path. Keep the first project read-only until those controls work.
lessons.example: Search a curated set of documents, compare two sources, and draft a cited summary for review.
lessons.challenge: Build the research agent and test normal, no-evidence, tool-error, and instruction-injection inputs.
lessons.takeaway: An agent project is its control system as much as its model prompt.

lessons.title: Evaluate and Demonstrate the Agent
lessons.objective: Show repeatable behavior and explain tool, state, and safety limits.
lessons.concept: Evaluation should record task success, evidence quality, unnecessary tool calls, stop behavior, and safe handling of adversarial input. A demo should not hide cases that fail or require human review.
lessons.example: Compare the planned and actual tool trace for a supported and unsupported research question.
lessons.challenge: Run five test cases, summarize results, and present one limitation with a specific improvement proposal.
lessons.takeaway: Measure agent behavior across traces, not just the final answer.

mcp_tool_connected_ai.title: MCP & Tool-Connected AI
mcp_tool_connected_ai.description: Connect AI applications to external capabilities using MCP concepts, server-provided tools/resources, and explicit permissions.

modules.title: Why Tool-Connected AI Matters
modules.description: Understand the boundary between model generation and external tools, data, and applications.
modules.story: A desktop assistant can explain a spreadsheet formula but cannot inspect the user's authorized workbook until connected to a capability.
modules.discovery: Identify what the model can infer and what requires an external, permissioned tool or resource.

lessons.title: Models Need Explicit Capabilities
lessons.objective: Explain why a model needs an application-mediated capability to access external systems.
lessons.concept: A language model generates outputs from provided context. Tool-connected applications expose bounded operations or resources and return results to the model; access remains controlled by the host and connected service.
lessons.example: An assistant can summarize a file only after a host provides its content through an authorized read operation.
lessons.challenge: List three requested assistant tasks and identify the external capability and permission each would require.
lessons.takeaway: Connection adds capability, not automatic trust or access.

lessons.title: MCP and Adjacent Integration Patterns
lessons.objective: Distinguish MCP from direct API calls and model function-calling schemas.
lessons.concept: MCP is a protocol for connecting AI applications with servers that expose capabilities such as tools, resources, and prompts. A direct API is an application-specific interface; function calling is a model interaction pattern and may be used inside an MCP-enabled host.
lessons.example: A host can discover an MCP server's tools, while a separate model call decides whether to propose one of those tools.
lessons.challenge: Classify four integration diagrams as direct API, function calling, MCP, or combinations and explain the protocol boundary.
lessons.takeaway: MCP standardizes a connection protocol; it is not itself a model or a generic synonym for APIs.

modules.title: MCP Concepts
modules.description: Learn host, client, server, capability discovery, and request-response concepts accurately.
modules.story: A team connects one desktop host to a local server and asks which component owns each decision.
modules.discovery: Trace the connection lifecycle and identify where discovery ends and authorization begins.

lessons.title: Hosts, Clients, and Servers
lessons.objective: Describe the roles of an MCP host, client connection, and MCP server.
lessons.concept: The host is the AI application, its MCP client manages a server connection, and the server exposes capabilities. The host coordinates model interaction and user experience; server behavior is bounded by its implementation and permissions.
lessons.example: A host opens a client connection to a calendar server and presents discovered calendar tools for possible use.
lessons.challenge: Draw the three roles for a sample desktop assistant and label which component prompts the user and which implements the operation.
lessons.takeaway: Keep protocol roles distinct from the model's decision-making role.

lessons.title: Capability Discovery and Lifecycle
lessons.objective: Explain how a client discovers capabilities and handles a server connection lifecycle.
lessons.concept: An MCP client establishes a session and discovers available server capabilities through protocol interactions. Capabilities can change or fail; clients should handle initialization, errors, and shutdown rather than assuming a permanent connection.
lessons.example: A host discovers a read-only project search tool, displays it, then reports that the server is unavailable when its process exits.
lessons.challenge: Write a lifecycle sequence with initialization, capability discovery, one request, a failure, and orderly shutdown.
lessons.takeaway: Discovery describes what a server offers; it does not grant every user permission to use it.

modules.title: Servers, Tools, and Resources
modules.description: Design server capabilities with clear schemas and understand the distinction between actions and context.
modules.story: A project server exposes a search action and repository documentation as context for an assistant.
modules.discovery: Compare a tool that performs an operation with a resource that provides information.

lessons.title: Expose Narrow Tools
lessons.objective: Define a tool name, input schema, result, and safe error behavior for an MCP server.
lessons.concept: Tools represent callable operations with declared inputs and results. Keep operations narrow, validate arguments in the server, and avoid exposing broad shell or database access when a specific action is sufficient.
lessons.example: Expose a `find_issue` tool with a bounded query and project scope rather than arbitrary SQL execution.
lessons.challenge: Design one read-only and one write-capable tool; specify how each validates caller scope and reports errors.
lessons.takeaway: A tool schema communicates shape; server checks enforce authority.

lessons.title: Publish Resources and Prompts
lessons.objective: Select when to provide a resource or reusable prompt rather than a tool action.
lessons.concept: Resources provide addressable context such as a document or data item. Prompts can package reusable interaction templates. Neither should be confused with an operation that changes external state.
lessons.example: Expose a versioned API guide as a resource and a “draft a release summary” template as a prompt; keep issue creation as a tool.
lessons.challenge: Classify five capabilities as tool, resource, or prompt and justify the user interaction each needs.
lessons.takeaway: Choose the capability type that matches its behavior and control needs.

modules.title: Connecting AI to Tools
modules.description: Connect a host to a server and mediate discovery, model selection, validation, and execution.
modules.story: The model proposes an issue-creation tool call after reading an issue report, but the user has not approved it.
modules.discovery: Trace a proposed call through the host and server instead of treating the model response as execution.

lessons.title: Tool Discovery and Model Interaction
lessons.objective: Explain how discovered MCP tools may be presented to a model and selected by an application.
lessons.concept: A host may translate discovered tool definitions into a model's tool-calling format. The model can propose a call; the host remains responsible for policy, user interaction, argument validation, and dispatch.
lessons.example: The model proposes `create_issue`; the host checks project access and asks for approval before sending the request to the MCP server.
lessons.challenge: Diagram discovery, model proposal, host validation, user approval, server execution, and returned result.
lessons.takeaway: A model tool call is a proposal routed through the host's controls.

lessons.title: Connect a Test Host and Server
lessons.objective: Configure a test connection and verify one bounded operation end to end.
lessons.concept: Connection setup depends on the host and transport. Verify the server identity, declared capabilities, expected inputs, and behavior on disconnect; never assume a server is trustworthy because it is discoverable.
lessons.example: Connect a local test host to a sample server that returns public documentation metadata only.
lessons.challenge: Run a read-only test operation and record the server, capability, request, result, and disconnect behavior.
lessons.takeaway: Test the entire host-client-server path using a least-privilege capability.

modules.title: Building an MCP Tool
modules.description: Implement a small protocol server capability with input validation, useful errors, and test coverage.
modules.story: A team wants an assistant to search approved internal guides without gaining arbitrary filesystem access.
modules.discovery: Define the smallest server capability that can answer the task and nothing broader.

lessons.title: Implement a Bounded Server Capability
lessons.objective: Build a small MCP tool or resource over a narrowly scoped data source.
lessons.concept: An MCP server implements protocol interactions and capability handlers. Validate input, restrict the data source, return structured results, and keep secrets and authorization checks outside model-generated arguments.
lessons.example: A guide-search tool accepts a query and returns title, section, and a short excerpt from a fixed approved directory.
lessons.challenge: Implement or sketch the capability and reject a path or scope that exceeds its configured boundary.
lessons.takeaway: The server is the enforcement point for its exposed capability.

lessons.title: Test Protocol and Capability Behavior
lessons.objective: Test valid requests, malformed input, server errors, and result shape.
lessons.concept: A server test should verify initialization, discovery, capability execution, validation, errors, and clean shutdown. Test actual protocol messages with a compatible client or harness rather than only calling the underlying helper.
lessons.example: Send a valid search request and one invalid empty query, then confirm the error is bounded and no filesystem details leak.
lessons.challenge: Create a test checklist for one capability and demonstrate success, invalid input, and unavailable data.
lessons.takeaway: Protocol compatibility and operation correctness are separate checks.

modules.title: Permissions and Security
modules.description: Apply least privilege, consent, secret handling, and trust boundaries to connected tools.
modules.story: A newly discovered server can read documents and send messages, but users need to know what it will do.
modules.discovery: Inventory the data and side effects each capability can reach before enabling it.

lessons.title: Least Privilege and User Consent
lessons.objective: Limit capability scope and require clear consent for sensitive or consequential operations.
lessons.concept: Authorize the user and operation at the host or server boundary. Make permissions specific, inspectable, and revocable; discovery alone is not consent to use a tool.
lessons.example: Allow a user to search a selected folder but require confirmation before sharing a document externally.
lessons.challenge: Create a permission matrix for three tools with read/write scope, user role, approval need, and revocation path.
lessons.takeaway: Permission should be explicit and no broader than the task requires.

lessons.title: Secrets, Untrusted Data, and Audit
lessons.objective: Protect credentials and keep retrieved tool data from changing system authority.
lessons.concept: Keep credentials in the host or server's secure configuration, not prompts or tool results. Treat returned content as untrusted data, validate actions independently, and log capability use with appropriate privacy limits.
lessons.example: A repository file may contain instructions to expose a token; the host should treat it as file content, never as authority.
lessons.challenge: Threat-model a connected assistant and identify one control for credential exposure, prompt injection, and unauthorized action.
lessons.takeaway: Protocol connectivity does not remove ordinary application security responsibilities.

modules.title: Debugging Tool Connections
modules.description: Diagnose initialization, discovery, transport, schema, and execution failures systematically.
modules.story: A host lists a tool but calls fail because the server expects a different argument shape.
modules.discovery: Compare protocol trace, declared schema, host request, and server response in order.

lessons.title: Trace a Connection Failure
lessons.objective: Localize a failure to connection, capability discovery, input validation, or execution.
lessons.concept: Inspect server startup, transport, initialization, capability list, request schema, and response. Stable request IDs and sanitized logs help correlate events without recording secrets.
lessons.example: A missing tool is a discovery problem; a tool returning an input error is a later-stage schema or validation problem.
lessons.challenge: Diagnose three sample failure traces and assign the earliest failing stage plus the next evidence to collect.
lessons.takeaway: Follow the protocol stages instead of changing prompts blindly.

lessons.title: Handle Version and Availability Changes
lessons.objective: Plan for server restarts, unavailable capabilities, and incompatible schema changes.
lessons.concept: Hosts should handle server disconnection and capability changes explicitly. Versioned contracts and compatibility checks reduce breakage when a server changes; users need a clear fallback when a capability is unavailable.
lessons.example: When a project server is offline, offer manual issue lookup rather than pretending the tool call succeeded.
lessons.challenge: Write a compatibility and recovery checklist for a server tool whose required input field changes.
lessons.takeaway: Connected capabilities are dependencies that can change or fail.

modules.title: Build a Tool-Connected AI Workflow
modules.description: Connect a host and server to complete a bounded workflow with visible permissions and outcomes.
modules.story: Create a project assistant that searches a guide, drafts a response, and waits before creating a task.
modules.discovery: Demonstrate the boundary between MCP protocol capability and the host's model/tool-call policy.

lessons.title: Assemble the Connected Workflow
lessons.objective: Build a host-server flow using a resource or read tool and one controlled action.
lessons.concept: The project joins capability discovery, model interaction, argument validation, user approval, server execution, and a traceable result. Keep the first action reversible or approval-gated.
lessons.example: Retrieve an approved guide section, draft a task from it, show the source and proposed fields, then create only after confirmation.
lessons.challenge: Build the flow and test a valid request, a denied permission, and a server-unavailable case.
lessons.takeaway: A connected workflow has both protocol behavior and application policy.

lessons.title: Present a Security and Protocol Review
lessons.objective: Explain the protocol roles, capability boundaries, and observed test behavior.
lessons.concept: A strong handoff states which component is host, client, and server; which capabilities were discovered; what data they can reach; what approvals apply; and what remains untested.
lessons.example: Show a trace where the model proposed a tool call but the host withheld it until the user approved.
lessons.challenge: Present a short review with a sequence diagram, permission matrix, and evidence from three tests.
lessons.takeaway: Accurate terminology and visible boundaries make tool-connected AI understandable.

ai_software_engineering.title: AI-Powered Software Engineering
ai_software_engineering.description: Apply AI across requirements, architecture, coding, testing, review, documentation, and release with engineering controls.

modules.title: AI in the Software Development Lifecycle
modules.description: Place AI assistance within a lifecycle that retains engineering ownership and review.
modules.story: A team speeds up code generation but discovers requirements and deployment checks still consume the same time.
modules.discovery: Map where AI can assist and where a person or deterministic check must remain accountable.

lessons.title: Lifecycle Tasks and AI Boundaries
lessons.objective: Identify useful AI assistance across planning, implementation, testing, and maintenance.
lessons.concept: AI can help draft, search, summarize, and propose changes across a lifecycle. It does not own product intent, permissions, verification, or production decisions; define a review boundary for each assisted task.
lessons.example: Use AI to summarize a failing test log, then confirm the diagnosis against the source and reproduce the failure.
lessons.challenge: Map five lifecycle activities to AI assistance, human responsibility, and an observable verification step.
lessons.takeaway: AI assistance is a tool inside engineering practice, not a replacement lifecycle.

lessons.title: Measure Workflow Impact
lessons.objective: Compare cycle time and defect risk before and after adding AI assistance.
lessons.concept: Measure the whole task, including prompt preparation, review, correction, tests, and rework. Faster first drafts may not shorten delivery if verification or defect rates worsen.
lessons.example: Track time from issue start to reviewed merge for similar small changes with and without AI assistance.
lessons.challenge: Choose two measures and design a small comparison that avoids treating raw generated lines as productivity.
lessons.takeaway: Evaluate AI by delivered, verified work rather than output volume.

modules.title: AI-Assisted Requirements
modules.description: Turn stakeholder language into traceable requirements, acceptance criteria, and edge cases.
modules.story: A stakeholder asks for “quick account recovery,” but the team has not defined identity proof or failure behavior.
modules.discovery: Use AI to surface questions and cases while keeping the source of each requirement visible.

lessons.title: Clarify User Needs and Constraints
lessons.objective: Use an assistant to identify ambiguity without inventing stakeholder decisions.
lessons.concept: AI can summarize interviews and propose clarifying questions. Preserve quotations or source links, separate confirmed needs from inferred themes, and ask stakeholders to decide unresolved policy.
lessons.example: Summarize account recovery interviews while labeling each claim with the interview note that supports it.
lessons.challenge: Convert a short interview into confirmed needs, open questions, and unsupported assumptions.
lessons.takeaway: AI can organize evidence but cannot supply missing product authority.

lessons.title: Acceptance Criteria and Edge Cases
lessons.objective: Generate and review testable acceptance criteria for normal and failure paths.
lessons.concept: Criteria should be observable and specific. An assistant can suggest boundary cases, but engineers must check feasibility, security, and consistency with existing contracts.
lessons.example: For a reset link, define expiry, reuse, invalid address, and rate-limit behavior.
lessons.challenge: Draft criteria for one feature, then remove any that are ambiguous or unsupported by the agreed requirements.
lessons.takeaway: Requirements become useful when behavior can be verified.

modules.title: AI-Assisted Architecture
modules.description: Use AI to compare design options against constraints, existing systems, and operational costs.
modules.story: An assistant recommends a new queue service without seeing the team's scale, deployment model, or reliability needs.
modules.discovery: Supply constraints and ask for tradeoffs rather than accepting a single confident design.

lessons.title: Generate and Compare Design Options
lessons.objective: Compare architecture options using explicit quality attributes and constraints.
lessons.concept: Ask for alternatives with assumptions, failure modes, cost, security, and migration impact. Validate claims against authoritative documentation and the repository's actual architecture.
lessons.example: Compare synchronous processing with a queue for bursty imports, including retry and duplicate-event behavior.
lessons.challenge: Create a decision matrix for two options and identify which assumptions need measurement or stakeholder confirmation.
lessons.takeaway: Architecture output is a hypothesis to evaluate against real constraints.

lessons.title: Document a Decision Record
lessons.objective: Record context, options, tradeoffs, and a reversible decision where possible.
lessons.concept: A decision record preserves why a choice was made, not just what was chosen. AI can draft the record from verified notes, but owners must check facts and unresolved risks.
lessons.example: Record why a team chose a managed queue and how it will monitor delivery delay and duplicate handling.
lessons.challenge: Write a one-page decision record with context, two options, tradeoffs, chosen direction, and revisit trigger.
lessons.takeaway: A clear decision record keeps assumptions visible to future maintainers.

modules.title: Code Generation
modules.description: Request small patches, inspect changes, and retain project conventions and security constraints.
modules.story: An assistant generates a helper that works locally but bypasses the application's shared validation function.
modules.discovery: Compare the patch to the existing codebase and the contract the new code must preserve.

lessons.title: Generate a Bounded Patch
lessons.objective: Ask for a focused implementation tied to a verified requirement and relevant code path.
lessons.concept: A bounded patch request names expected behavior, relevant files, constraints, and checks. Generate incrementally so each change can be reviewed and tested before adding another layer.
lessons.example: Ask for a parser change in one module that preserves the existing API response and reuses its validation helper.
lessons.challenge: Prepare a small patch request and compare generated changes with the project conventions and stated non-goals.
lessons.takeaway: Small patches make generated changes easier to understand.

lessons.title: Inspect Dependencies and Security
lessons.objective: Check generated code for unsafe inputs, secrets, permissions, and unnecessary dependencies.
lessons.concept: Generated code may introduce vulnerable patterns or packages. Review data flow, escaping, authorization, secret handling, dependency provenance, and whether a simpler existing utility already solves the task.
lessons.example: Reject a generated client-side API key and move the call behind the existing server boundary.
lessons.challenge: Review a sample patch with a new dependency and user-controlled input; list required changes before approval.
lessons.takeaway: A clean-looking diff can still cross a security boundary.

modules.title: Debugging with AI
modules.description: Use logs and reproductions to get targeted hypotheses, then verify the cause and fix.
modules.story: A deployment error appears only with one input size, while the assistant suggests an unrelated rewrite.
modules.discovery: Provide reproducible evidence and ask for a testable diagnosis rather than a broad patch.

lessons.title: Turn Evidence into a Diagnosis
lessons.objective: Supply minimal logs, steps, and code context to investigate a failure.
lessons.concept: A useful debugging request includes expected and actual results, reproduction steps, environment, and relevant traces. Remove secrets and unrelated data before sharing logs.
lessons.example: Show a timeout trace, request size, and one failing input while redacting tokens and customer details.
lessons.challenge: Create a minimal bug report from a sample failure and identify what evidence is missing before changing code.
lessons.takeaway: A grounded diagnosis begins with a reproducible observation.

lessons.title: Verify Root Cause and Regression
lessons.objective: Test the proposed cause and confirm the fix does not break adjacent behavior.
lessons.concept: A suggested fix should predict an observable change. Reproduce before and after, inspect the diff, and add a regression check that fails for the old behavior.
lessons.example: If oversized input triggers a timeout, vary size around the boundary and verify a bounded validation response.
lessons.challenge: Design a minimal experiment for a proposed bug cause and add one regression case for the confirmed failure.
lessons.takeaway: Explanation is not evidence until the predicted behavior is observed.

modules.title: Testing with AI
modules.description: Use AI to propose test ideas while preserving independent expected results and meaningful coverage.
modules.story: A generated test suite passes because its expected values repeat the implementation's mistaken assumption.
modules.discovery: Separate test generation from the source of truth for expected behavior.

lessons.title: Generate Test Cases from Contracts
lessons.objective: Derive normal, boundary, and invalid cases from an existing specification.
lessons.concept: An assistant can enumerate partitions and edge cases from a contract. Review whether each case reflects intended behavior; avoid accepting tests that merely mirror the code under test.
lessons.example: For a 1-to-5 rating endpoint, test both endpoints, values outside the range, non-integers, and missing answers.
lessons.challenge: Generate a case table from a function contract and identify the authoritative expected outcome for each row.
lessons.takeaway: Test ideas are useful only when expected behavior comes from a trusted contract.

lessons.title: Review Test Quality
lessons.objective: Check that tests fail for the defect they claim to detect and cover meaningful behavior.
lessons.concept: A strong test asserts outcomes at the right boundary and detects a regression. Review setup, assertions, fixtures, isolation, and whether a passing test could still permit the reported bug.
lessons.example: Temporarily restore a stale-cache defect and verify the new test fails before accepting the fix.
lessons.challenge: Mutation-check two generated tests by changing the target behavior and confirming each test catches the change.
lessons.takeaway: A test that never fails on the defect offers little protection.

modules.title: Code Review and Refactoring
modules.description: Use AI to explain code and propose refactors while protecting behavior and reviewability.
modules.story: A large generated refactor changes naming, control flow, and an error response in one patch.
modules.discovery: Reduce the change to behavior-preserving steps and compare observable contracts.

lessons.title: Review a Generated Change
lessons.objective: Review scope, invariants, error behavior, and maintainability in an AI-assisted diff.
lessons.concept: Review the diff against a requirement and existing invariants. Ask what behavior changed, which error paths moved, and whether the patch introduces hidden coupling or unnecessary abstraction.
lessons.example: A refactor of a date parser must preserve timezone handling and invalid-date responses across all callers.
lessons.challenge: Review a sample refactor and write one comment tied to a behavior or invariant, not personal style alone.
lessons.takeaway: Review protects contracts as well as code quality.

lessons.title: Refactor in Behavior-Preserving Steps
lessons.objective: Break a broad refactor into small steps protected by tests and readable diffs.
lessons.concept: Refactoring changes structure without intended behavior change. Establish current behavior, make one structural step, rerun relevant checks, and avoid mixing feature changes into the same patch.
lessons.example: Extract one pure validation helper, preserve call order, and rerun tests before changing the next module.
lessons.challenge: Split a proposed multi-file refactor into three reviewable commits with a verification check after each.
lessons.takeaway: Small verified refactors limit the cost of a wrong assumption.

modules.title: Documentation
modules.description: Create accurate documentation from verified behavior, contracts, and operational evidence.
modules.story: A generated README describes environment variables and endpoints that no longer exist.
modules.discovery: Check documentation claims against source, configuration, and a real execution path.

lessons.title: Document APIs and Setup
lessons.objective: Document a setup path and API contract with verified names, methods, and responses.
lessons.concept: Documentation should identify prerequisites, configuration, safe examples, required authorization, input/output shape, and common errors. Avoid copying secrets or presenting inferred behavior as fact.
lessons.example: Document an authenticated endpoint with one redacted request and its actual success and unauthorized responses.
lessons.challenge: Write a setup section from the repository and verify each command and environment name before retaining it.
lessons.takeaway: Documentation is another interface that must match the implementation.

lessons.title: Use AI to Maintain Documentation Safely
lessons.objective: Update documentation from a reviewed change without inventing unsupported behavior.
lessons.concept: AI can identify likely documentation touchpoints from a diff. Verify each statement against code or observed behavior, distinguish limitations, and remove obsolete instructions rather than appending contradictory notes.
lessons.example: After a response field changes, update the API example and confirm the server actually returns that field.
lessons.challenge: Generate a documentation update from a sample diff, then annotate every claim with its source of verification.
lessons.takeaway: Documentation maintenance needs traceable evidence.

modules.title: Shipping with AI
modules.description: Release AI-assisted changes with secret hygiene, review, deployment checks, and rollback awareness.
modules.story: A feature passes tests locally but fails after deployment because configuration differs and a token entered the commit.
modules.discovery: Review operational assumptions and secret boundaries before merging or deploying.

lessons.title: Release and Configuration Checks
lessons.objective: Prepare a release checklist for configuration, migrations, checks, and runtime behavior.
lessons.concept: A release must account for build and runtime configuration, data compatibility, tests, observability, and rollback. AI-generated deployment scripts still require review against the actual environment.
lessons.example: Verify a required model key is injected server-side and the app returns a clear service error if it is absent.
lessons.challenge: Create a release checklist for your feature and test one configuration-missing case in a safe environment.
lessons.takeaway: Release readiness is verified in the environment that will run the code.

lessons.title: Secrets and Rollback
lessons.objective: Prevent credential exposure and plan a reversible rollout for a risky change.
lessons.concept: Secrets belong in managed configuration, not source, prompts, screenshots, or logs. A rollback plan names the prior version and any data changes that make reversal more complex.
lessons.example: Deploy a feature behind an existing server-controlled setting and confirm logs do not print the provider key.
lessons.challenge: Inspect a sample release diff for secret leaks and write a rollback plan including any data compatibility constraints.
lessons.takeaway: Protect credentials and plan recovery before users depend on a release.

modules.title: AI Engineering Project
modules.description: Complete an engineering change from requirements through release evidence using AI as a reviewed assistant.
modules.story: A small team asks you to improve a real feature without changing its established contract.
modules.discovery: Demonstrate how requirement, patch, tests, review, documentation, and release checks connect.

lessons.title: Deliver the Engineering Change
lessons.objective: Implement and verify a bounded feature with a traceable requirement and reviewable diff.
lessons.concept: The project uses AI for selected tasks while keeping requirements, data boundaries, tests, and deployment decisions explicit. Preserve existing interfaces unless a confirmed requirement calls for a change.
lessons.example: Add a validated export option, protect its access boundary, and keep the existing response shape for callers that do not request it.
lessons.challenge: Deliver the feature with acceptance checks, an inspected diff, boundary tests, and an updated API or user guide.
lessons.takeaway: Engineering quality comes from the complete change path, not the generated patch alone.

lessons.title: Present Review Evidence
lessons.objective: Explain the implementation, verification, risks, and remaining work to another engineer.
lessons.concept: A handoff should cover the requirement, changed paths, tests and results, operational assumptions, known limitations, and rollback or recovery notes. Be explicit about checks not performed.
lessons.example: Show one successful test, one rejected input, the relevant diff, and the deployment configuration used.
lessons.challenge: Prepare a five-minute technical review with evidence and one honest limitation.
lessons.takeaway: A clear handoff makes the change maintainable by someone else.

ai_evaluation.title: AI Evaluation & Reliability
ai_evaluation.description: Evaluate AI behavior with representative cases, groundedness checks, regression suites, safety controls, and operational monitoring.

modules.title: Why AI Systems Fail
modules.description: Classify failures across data, retrieval, prompts, models, tools, and product boundaries.
modules.story: A customer assistant gives a useful answer in a demo but invents an account status in production.
modules.discovery: Trace the failure to a system stage before blaming the model as a whole.

lessons.title: Failure Modes Across the System
lessons.objective: Identify distinct causes of an incorrect or unsafe AI result.
lessons.concept: Failures can come from missing or stale data, poor retrieval, ambiguous instructions, model limitations, tool errors, validation gaps, or user-interface framing. A useful diagnosis locates the earliest stage where expected behavior diverged.
lessons.example: A wrong policy answer may begin with retrieval selecting an outdated version, even if the model summarizes it faithfully.
lessons.challenge: Classify six failure examples by earliest failing stage and name the evidence needed to confirm each cause.
lessons.takeaway: Treat the AI feature as a system with multiple failure boundaries.

lessons.title: Impact, Severity, and Triage
lessons.objective: Prioritize failures by user impact, likelihood, reversibility, and exposure.
lessons.concept: Triage considers who is affected, how often the failure occurs, whether harm is reversible, and whether data or access boundaries are crossed. Severity should guide escalation and release decisions, not just a model score.
lessons.example: A typo in an internal summary differs in severity from exposing another user's private record.
lessons.challenge: Rank four failure reports with a severity rubric and justify which requires immediate disablement or escalation.
lessons.takeaway: Prioritize by impact and boundary violations, not by how surprising a response looks.

modules.title: Evaluation Fundamentals
modules.description: Define intended behavior, measurable criteria, representative data, and review procedures.
modules.story: Two reviewers disagree whether an answer is “good” because the team has no shared rubric.
modules.discovery: Turn a subjective quality label into observable criteria and examples.

lessons.title: Define the Evaluation Target
lessons.objective: State the user task and the behavior the evaluation is meant to measure.
lessons.concept: Evaluation begins with a defined target such as factual support, task completion, safe refusal, or tool accuracy. A single score rarely represents all quality dimensions or product suitability.
lessons.example: For a cited support answer, separately measure whether it answers the question, uses current policy, and cites the right section.
lessons.challenge: Write an evaluation target and three separate quality dimensions for one AI feature.
lessons.takeaway: Measure the behavior that matters to the user and risk owner.

lessons.title: Build a Consistent Rubric
lessons.objective: Create anchored scoring rules that different reviewers can apply similarly.
lessons.concept: A rubric defines criteria, score anchors, examples, and treatment of unanswerable cases. Calibrate reviewers on shared samples and record disagreement rather than hiding it in an average.
lessons.example: Score citation support as supported, partially supported, unsupported, or no relevant evidence with one example per label.
lessons.challenge: Draft a four-level rubric and ask a second reviewer to score the same five outputs; discuss disagreements.
lessons.takeaway: Clear anchors improve consistency but do not remove judgment.

modules.title: Designing Test Cases
modules.description: Build a representative evaluation set that covers common use, boundaries, ambiguity, and misuse.
modules.story: A model passes the team's three hand-picked happy paths and fails on normal user phrasing.
modules.discovery: Expand test coverage from examples to meaningful input categories and risks.

lessons.title: Representative and Boundary Cases
lessons.objective: Sample typical, rare, incomplete, conflicting, and out-of-scope inputs.
lessons.concept: A useful set reflects real traffic or carefully stated user scenarios. Include paraphrases, missing context, boundaries, and cases with no valid answer; avoid relying on a few convenient demonstrations.
lessons.example: Test both “reset my password” and “I cannot access my account,” plus an expired-link scenario.
lessons.challenge: Create a stratified test list with at least one typical, boundary, ambiguous, and out-of-scope case.
lessons.takeaway: Coverage comes from the range of situations, not the size of a happy-path list.

lessons.title: Label Data and Record Provenance
lessons.objective: Store expected behavior, source evidence, and test-set version with each case.
lessons.concept: Evaluation records should include input, expected outcome or evidence, label source, permissions context, and version. Protect private examples and ensure reviewers can reproduce the label decision.
lessons.example: A policy answer case stores the expected section ID and policy version rather than copying confidential user details.
lessons.challenge: Design a case record format and add provenance to three sample cases.
lessons.takeaway: A test case is only useful if its expected result can be explained.

modules.title: Accuracy, Relevance, and Grounding
modules.description: Check correctness, usefulness, evidence support, and citation behavior as separate properties.
modules.story: A fluent answer cites a relevant document but reverses the rule described in it.
modules.discovery: Score the claim and its evidence independently from writing quality.

lessons.title: Factual Accuracy and Relevance
lessons.objective: Distinguish a correct answer from one that is merely related or well written.
lessons.concept: Accuracy asks whether claims are correct for the task; relevance asks whether the response addresses the user's question. Evaluate both against trusted references or explicit criteria.
lessons.example: A response about account security may be accurate but irrelevant when the user asked how to change notification settings.
lessons.challenge: Score five sample outputs for accuracy and relevance separately and explain one disagreement.
lessons.takeaway: A useful response must be both correct and responsive.

lessons.title: Grounding and Citation Checks
lessons.objective: Verify that each factual claim is supported by the cited source and its qualifications.
lessons.concept: Grounding review links answer claims to source passages and checks whether wording preserves caveats, dates, and scope. Citation presence alone does not show that the claim follows from the source.
lessons.example: A citation to a policy section is insufficient if the answer omits the section's eligibility exception.
lessons.challenge: Annotate claims in a sample answer with supporting, partial, or absent evidence and rewrite unsupported claims.
lessons.takeaway: Check what the source supports, not just whether a source is attached.

modules.title: LLM Evaluation
modules.description: Use human review and carefully constrained automated evaluators to assess generated outputs.
modules.story: A model grader assigns high scores to verbose answers even when they contain unsupported details.
modules.discovery: Test an evaluator against human-labeled examples before using its judgments at scale.

lessons.title: Human Evaluation and Calibration
lessons.objective: Organize review so raters apply a rubric consistently and expose uncertainty.
lessons.concept: Human review is valuable for nuanced quality and safety judgments. Use clear rubrics, calibrated examples, appropriate privacy, and an adjudication process for disagreements.
lessons.example: Two reviewers independently judge whether a generated explanation follows a source, then reconcile the disputed claim.
lessons.challenge: Double-score six outputs and calculate simple agreement by rubric dimension; inspect where instructions were unclear.
lessons.takeaway: Reviewer disagreement can reveal an unclear criterion or a genuinely ambiguous case.

lessons.title: Automated Judges and Their Limits
lessons.objective: Use an automated evaluator only after checking bias, stability, and alignment with the target.
lessons.concept: LLM judges can scale rubric checks but may favor their own style, miss subtle errors, or vary across runs. Compare them with human labels and keep high-impact decisions out of an unchecked judge.
lessons.example: Compare a judge's citation-support labels with expert review on a held-out set including misleading citations.
lessons.challenge: Create a judge prompt, evaluate it on ten labeled cases, and report false positives and false negatives.
lessons.takeaway: An evaluator is another system that requires evaluation.

modules.title: Regression Testing
modules.description: Protect known behavior as prompts, models, data, tools, and application code change.
modules.story: A new model improves concise answers but starts ignoring the application's required uncertainty message.
modules.discovery: Keep a fixed comparison set and track changes by behavior dimension.

lessons.title: Version the Evaluation Baseline
lessons.objective: Record model, prompt, retrieval, dataset, and evaluator versions for a repeatable comparison.
lessons.concept: A result is meaningful only with its system configuration and test-set version. Preserve a baseline and note stochastic settings, provider changes, and data updates that affect reproducibility.
lessons.example: Compare two prompt versions on the same cases using the same model version and rubric.
lessons.challenge: Create a run record schema and compare two runs while holding all but one component constant.
lessons.takeaway: Version the conditions needed to interpret an evaluation result.

lessons.title: Detect Regressions and Tradeoffs
lessons.objective: Identify behavior changes and decide which require correction or escalation.
lessons.concept: Aggregate metrics can conceal regressions for one user group or failure type. Inspect per-category results and critical cases, define acceptable thresholds, and review tradeoffs before release.
lessons.example: Overall accuracy rises while the system's abstention behavior worsens on questions with missing evidence.
lessons.challenge: Analyze a small before-and-after score table and identify one release blocker hidden by the aggregate.
lessons.takeaway: Averages should not erase high-impact failures.

modules.title: Safety and Reliability
modules.description: Test refusal, access boundaries, robustness, and safe behavior during dependency failures.
modules.story: A model is asked for data outside the user's permissions and responds with a convincing fabricated record.
modules.discovery: Test the authorization and fallback system, not just the prompt's request to behave safely.

lessons.title: Safety Cases and Permission Boundaries
lessons.objective: Test that policy and access controls hold under direct and indirect attempts to bypass them.
lessons.concept: Safety checks include allowed and disallowed tasks, cross-user access, prompt injection, and tool authorization. Enforce permissions in trusted systems rather than relying only on model instructions.
lessons.example: A model may summarize records only after the server filters them to the authenticated user's scope.
lessons.challenge: Create test cases for denied content, unauthorized records, and injected tool instructions; define expected system behavior.
lessons.takeaway: Security boundaries must hold even when a model response is wrong.

lessons.title: Reliability Under Degraded Conditions
lessons.objective: Verify fallback and recovery when models, tools, or retrieval systems fail.
lessons.concept: Dependency failure should produce bounded retries, a safe unavailable state, or a human path. Avoid presenting stale cached output as current unless its age and source are clear.
lessons.example: If retrieval is unavailable, tell the user the answer cannot be verified instead of generating from general model memory.
lessons.challenge: Simulate one provider timeout and one retrieval failure; verify the response, logging, and recovery path.
lessons.takeaway: Reliable systems make degradation visible and recoverable.

modules.title: Monitoring AI Systems
modules.description: Observe quality, safety, latency, usage, and drift after deployment with privacy-conscious telemetry.
modules.story: A quality metric stays flat while complaints cluster around one newly added document type.
modules.discovery: Segment monitoring signals enough to find meaningful changes without collecting unnecessary user content.

lessons.title: Operational and Quality Signals
lessons.objective: Select indicators for service health, output quality, user feedback, and cost.
lessons.concept: Monitor latency, errors, usage, tool failures, review outcomes, feedback, and sampled quality checks. Define alert thresholds and owners; a single uptime metric cannot show whether answers remain useful.
lessons.example: Track citation-open rate alongside weekly human review of sampled citation support.
lessons.challenge: Build a dashboard outline with five signals, threshold rationale, data owner, and response action.
lessons.takeaway: Monitoring should connect a signal to an accountable response.

lessons.title: Privacy-Conscious Drift Review
lessons.objective: Detect changes in input or output patterns without retaining excessive sensitive content.
lessons.concept: Distribution shift can change performance as users, documents, or model behavior change. Sample and redact data carefully, track category-level changes, and re-evaluate when a drift signal crosses a defined threshold.
lessons.example: Monitor the share of questions with no retrieved evidence by category, using hashed request IDs rather than raw conversations.
lessons.challenge: Write a drift response plan with a signal, privacy control, evaluation trigger, and owner.
lessons.takeaway: Observe change while collecting only what is needed to respond.

modules.title: Build an Evaluation System
modules.description: Create a repeatable evaluation pipeline with labeled cases, reports, thresholds, and review ownership.
modules.story: A team needs to decide whether a new assistant version is ready without relying on a single demo.
modules.discovery: Trace a test case through execution, scoring, review, reporting, and release decision.

lessons.title: Assemble the Evaluation Pipeline
lessons.objective: Run a versioned test set and produce per-dimension results with traceable evidence.
lessons.concept: The system loads versioned cases, invokes a fixed configuration, records outputs safely, scores defined criteria, and flags cases needing human review. Keep raw secrets and unnecessary personal data out of reports.
lessons.example: Run a retrieval assistant's known queries and emit separate retrieval recall, citation support, and refusal results.
lessons.challenge: Build a small evaluation runner or documented manual pipeline for ten cases and produce a versioned report.
lessons.takeaway: Repeatable evaluations turn quality discussions into inspectable evidence.

lessons.title: Set Release Gates and Report Limits
lessons.objective: Define thresholds and review rules for release decisions without overstating certainty.
lessons.concept: A release gate combines critical-case requirements, aggregate measures, subgroup checks, and human review. Thresholds reflect impact and product needs; passing a finite test set does not prove universal safety.
lessons.example: Block release on any cross-user access failure, while reviewing a modest change in average style scores separately.
lessons.challenge: Write a release gate with one hard blocker, two monitored thresholds, an owner, and a limitation statement.
lessons.takeaway: Evaluation informs a decision; it does not guarantee future behavior.

ai_builder_capstone.title: AI Builder Capstone
ai_builder_capstone.description: Plan, build, evaluate, secure, deploy, and demonstrate an AI application chosen around a real user problem.

modules.title: Choose the Problem
modules.description: Select a bounded, useful problem and test whether AI is warranted.
modules.story: A team starts with a preferred model and searches for a problem to justify it.
modules.discovery: Start with user friction and compare an AI approach with a simpler rule-based or manual alternative.

lessons.title: Find a Real, Bounded Problem
lessons.objective: Describe a recurring user problem, its current workaround, and the cost of leaving it unsolved.
lessons.concept: A capstone problem should have a reachable user, an observable outcome, and a bounded scope. Avoid choosing a solution before understanding the task and its constraints.
lessons.example: Learners spend time searching approved course notes for cited explanations; the current workaround is manual keyword search.
lessons.challenge: Interview or observe one potential user and write the problem, current workaround, frequency, and evidence.
lessons.takeaway: A credible project begins with a user problem, not an AI feature label.

lessons.title: Decide Whether AI Adds Value
lessons.objective: Compare AI with a deterministic workflow using quality, cost, and failure impact.
lessons.concept: AI is useful when language variability or unstructured inputs create value that simpler methods cannot provide affordably. Evaluate error consequences, review needs, data access, and operating cost.
lessons.example: A fixed form may be better than a model for calculating a known fee, while summarizing varied feedback may benefit from language generation.
lessons.challenge: Compare AI and non-AI approaches for your problem and record the evidence that would change your choice.
lessons.takeaway: Use AI when its contribution is clear and its risks can be bounded.

modules.title: Define the User
modules.description: Specify the primary user, their workflow, data boundaries, and success criteria.
modules.story: A project says “help students” but never distinguishes learners, instructors, or administrators.
modules.discovery: Name one primary user and follow their task from trigger to outcome.

lessons.title: User, Context, and Workflow
lessons.objective: Describe a primary user and the context in which the project will be used.
lessons.concept: A useful user definition includes goals, current steps, constraints, devices, permissions, and points where a wrong answer matters. Keep secondary audiences out of the first scope unless essential.
lessons.example: A learner on a phone needs a source-backed answer while studying; an instructor needs review controls that are not in the first learner flow.
lessons.challenge: Map the primary user's current workflow and identify one decision point and one failure point.
lessons.takeaway: Design for a specific real workflow before expanding audiences.

lessons.title: Success Criteria and Non-Goals
lessons.objective: Set measurable project outcomes and document what the capstone will not do.
lessons.concept: Success criteria should be observable and tied to the user's task. Non-goals prevent scope growth into unverified features, sensitive decisions, or unsupported integrations.
lessons.example: Success may mean users find the correct source section in under two minutes; automated grading is a non-goal.
lessons.challenge: Write three acceptance criteria, two non-goals, and a simple way to observe each criterion.
lessons.takeaway: A clear boundary makes a capstone finishable and testable.

modules.title: Design the AI System
modules.description: Choose model, data, retrieval, tools, state, and control boundaries for the selected problem.
modules.story: A diagram puts one model in the center and leaves data access, user permissions, and recovery unspecified.
modules.discovery: Trace trust boundaries and failure routes before committing to a component list.

lessons.title: Draw the Data and Component Flow
lessons.objective: Diagram user input, application code, model, data sources, tools, and outputs.
lessons.concept: A system diagram should show data direction, trust boundaries, identity, external dependencies, and side effects. Label which components validate and authorize requests.
lessons.example: A server authenticates a learner, retrieves permitted course sections, calls a model, checks citations, and returns a draft answer.
lessons.challenge: Draw your system with at least one failure path and identify where each data boundary is enforced.
lessons.takeaway: Architecture is a map of responsibilities and trust, not just boxes.

lessons.title: Choose a Small Technical Plan
lessons.objective: Select components and a staged build plan that match the project's constraints.
lessons.concept: Choose the least complex model, storage, and tool setup that can test the user outcome. Record assumptions, alternatives, integration risks, and an exit path if a dependency is unavailable.
lessons.example: Prototype retrieval over a small local corpus before committing to a hosted vector service.
lessons.challenge: Write a one-page design with components, alternatives, costs or constraints, and staged checkpoints.
lessons.takeaway: Build the smallest architecture that can test the project's central assumption.

modules.title: Build the Prototype
modules.description: Implement a complete, narrow user journey with visible behavior and clear limits.
modules.story: A polished landing page hides that the core task still returns sample text rather than real results.
modules.discovery: Complete one data path end to end and label any prototype-only behavior honestly.

lessons.title: Build the Core User Journey
lessons.objective: Implement one end-to-end user task with real inputs and an observable result.
lessons.concept: A prototype should prove the most important workflow, not simulate every feature. Keep the data path, user feedback, and failure states visible so assumptions can be tested.
lessons.example: A knowledge assistant accepts a question, retrieves actual approved passages, and presents a draft with source links.
lessons.challenge: Build the narrow core journey and demonstrate one successful and one invalid-input path.
lessons.takeaway: A real thin slice tests more than a broad mockup.

lessons.title: Inspect and Iterate
lessons.objective: Use user observation and execution traces to improve one verified friction point.
lessons.concept: Observe users completing the task and collect specific failures. Choose one change tied to evidence, inspect the diff, and retest; avoid changing several unrelated assumptions at once.
lessons.example: Users miss citations below the fold, so move source links next to the answer and observe whether they can verify it.
lessons.challenge: Run a short usability session, record one observed problem, implement a targeted revision, and retest the same task.
lessons.takeaway: Iteration should respond to observed behavior.

modules.title: Connect Tools and Data
modules.description: Add only the integrations required by the use case and enforce access and action boundaries.
modules.story: The prototype needs one approved data source and one optional action, but not access to the whole environment.
modules.discovery: Grant the smallest capability that completes the user task and verify its owner.

lessons.title: Connect an Authoritative Data Source
lessons.objective: Integrate a real source with identity, freshness, and provenance metadata.
lessons.concept: Data connectors should identify the authoritative source, enforce permissions, handle unavailable records, and retain source identifiers. Do not treat user-supplied text as trusted reference data.
lessons.example: Fetch a course lesson only after checking that the caller may access it, then attach lesson ID and update time to retrieved text.
lessons.challenge: Connect one source and test an allowed record, a missing record, and an unauthorized record.
lessons.takeaway: A useful answer starts with data the user is permitted to access.

lessons.title: Add a Tool with an Approval Boundary
lessons.objective: Integrate a narrow tool and require review before any consequential side effect.
lessons.concept: Tool arguments require validation and authorization in trusted code. Writes and external messages may need explicit approval, idempotency, and clear confirmation of the final action.
lessons.example: Prepare a draft task from a report and ask the owner to approve before creating it in a project tracker.
lessons.challenge: Add one read or draft capability and specify permission, approval, retry, and duplicate-action handling.
lessons.takeaway: Connected tools should be bounded by what the task actually needs.

modules.title: Test and Evaluate
modules.description: Test user outcomes, model behavior, retrieval, edge cases, and failure handling.
modules.story: The app works on its creator's sample but fails when a user asks an incomplete or unsupported question.
modules.discovery: Build a small test set before tuning the prompt or changing the model.

lessons.title: Create the Project Test Set
lessons.objective: Cover typical, boundary, missing-evidence, and failure cases for the core task.
lessons.concept: A test set should reflect the user's task and system boundaries. Record expected behavior and source evidence; separate retrieval, generation, tool, and interface results where possible.
lessons.example: Include a normal knowledge query, an unsupported question, a stale-source case, and a provider timeout.
lessons.challenge: Create and run at least eight cases across normal use, edge inputs, unsupported requests, and dependency failure.
lessons.takeaway: Test the user outcome and the paths where the system should not proceed.

lessons.title: Review Results and Set a Release Gate
lessons.objective: Summarize evidence and define blockers before moving the prototype forward.
lessons.concept: A release gate should specify critical failures that block release, quality measures to monitor, and human review requirements. Report sample size and untested areas rather than claiming universal reliability.
lessons.example: Any cross-user access failure blocks release; citation support is reviewed on a defined sample before a pilot.
lessons.challenge: Write a release decision from your test report with one blocker rule, one quality threshold, and one limitation.
lessons.takeaway: A release decision should be explainable from observed evidence.

modules.title: Improve and Secure
modules.description: Reduce failure impact with privacy, validation, access controls, and threat-informed testing.
modules.story: A demo uses realistic personal data and accepts model-generated actions without checking user permissions.
modules.discovery: Threat-model the path from user input to data retrieval and side effects.

lessons.title: Threat Model the AI Workflow
lessons.objective: Identify assets, trust boundaries, misuse cases, and mitigations for the capstone.
lessons.concept: Threat modeling considers data exposure, prompt injection, unauthorized access, tool abuse, and dependency compromise. Turn each threat into a control and a test rather than relying on a general safety statement.
lessons.example: A retrieved document attempts to instruct the model to reveal another user's record; server-side scope filtering prevents retrieval of that record.
lessons.challenge: Create a small threat table with asset, threat, control, verification test, and owner.
lessons.takeaway: Security improves when risks map to concrete controls and tests.

lessons.title: Privacy, Validation, and Safe Fallbacks
lessons.objective: Minimize sensitive data and reject outputs or actions that fail application rules.
lessons.concept: Send only task-relevant information, validate model and tool results, keep secrets out of prompts and logs, and offer a safe fallback when evidence or dependencies are missing.
lessons.example: If an answer has no valid citation, display a search failure and ask the user to narrow the query rather than inventing a source.
lessons.challenge: Review one end-to-end data path and add a privacy reduction, validation check, and safe fallback.
lessons.takeaway: Safety is enforced across data, tools, and interface behavior.

modules.title: Deploy
modules.description: Prepare configuration, monitoring, rollback, and an appropriately scoped pilot.
modules.story: A working prototype needs a first real user group, but the team has no way to observe or disable a harmful behavior.
modules.discovery: Make the deployment observable and reversible before widening access.

lessons.title: Prepare the Deployment
lessons.objective: Check runtime configuration, secrets, dependencies, and operational ownership.
lessons.concept: Deployment readiness includes server-side secrets, data permissions, health checks, dependency behavior, and an identified operator. Keep test and production data separate and document the supported environment.
lessons.example: Deploy a limited pilot with an environment-provided model key and a health check that reports provider configuration without exposing it.
lessons.challenge: Prepare a deployment checklist and verify a missing-secret and unavailable-provider case in a safe environment.
lessons.takeaway: A deployable app includes its operational requirements.

lessons.title: Pilot, Monitor, and Roll Back
lessons.objective: Plan a narrow pilot with quality signals, an owner, and a rollback trigger.
lessons.concept: A pilot limits exposure while collecting useful feedback. Define who monitors, what signals trigger pause, how to disable a feature, and how users are informed if service is unavailable.
lessons.example: Enable an assistant for one internal group and pause it if source citations fail a review threshold.
lessons.challenge: Write a pilot plan with audience, duration, signals, pause rule, and rollback steps.
lessons.takeaway: Start small and make stopping the feature a planned operation.

modules.title: Document
modules.description: Prepare technical, user, and operator documentation grounded in what the capstone actually does.
modules.story: A teammate inherits the project and cannot reproduce the demo or tell which limitations are intentional.
modules.discovery: Write the handoff so a new person can run, evaluate, and safely change the system.

lessons.title: Technical and User Documentation
lessons.objective: Document setup, data flow, supported tasks, and user-visible limitations.
lessons.concept: Technical docs explain architecture, configuration, contracts, and tests. User docs explain the task, source behavior, privacy boundaries, and what to do when an answer is unavailable.
lessons.example: Document which documents the assistant can search and how users can report a wrong citation.
lessons.challenge: Write a setup guide and one-page user guide, then ask another person to follow each without verbal help.
lessons.takeaway: Documentation should describe actual behavior in language suited to its audience.

lessons.title: Operations and Maintenance Handoff
lessons.objective: Record monitoring, source updates, recovery, and known technical debt.
lessons.concept: An operator handoff names the owner, required configuration, alert response, backup or rollback, source refresh process, and unresolved risks. It should distinguish verified steps from planned improvements.
lessons.example: Record how to re-index a changed source and rerun the retrieval regression set before publishing it.
lessons.challenge: Create an operations note and verify one recovery procedure with a teammate.
lessons.takeaway: A maintainable project has an explicit next owner and recovery path.

modules.title: Demo Day and Final Project
modules.description: Demonstrate the chosen AI application, explain evidence and limitations, and share a clear next-step plan.
modules.story: A reviewer sees the finished demo and asks what happens when the model is wrong or the data source is unavailable.
modules.discovery: Tell the project story from user problem to measured behavior, including the places where the system stops.

lessons.title: Prepare the Demonstration
lessons.objective: Plan a concise demo that shows the user task, evidence, and a meaningful failure path.
lessons.concept: A credible demo uses representative data, a repeatable path, and clear transitions between live behavior and explanation. Show sources, controls, and limitations instead of implying the system handles every case.
lessons.example: Demonstrate a supported research question with citations, then an unsupported query that correctly asks for more information.
lessons.challenge: Rehearse a five-minute walkthrough with one normal case, one boundary case, and the project's test evidence.
lessons.takeaway: A demonstration should show both capability and boundaries.

lessons.title: Present Results and Future Work
lessons.objective: Summarize user value, evaluation evidence, risks, and a prioritized next step.
lessons.concept: A final review states what was built, who it helps, what was tested, what remains uncertain, and which next improvement has the highest value. Avoid claiming guaranteed outcomes or universal accuracy.
lessons.example: Report that a small test set found a citation failure rate and explain how the team will measure it in a pilot.
lessons.challenge: Present a project summary with measured results, one known limitation, and a scoped next experiment.
lessons.takeaway: A strong capstone closes with evidence and a responsible path forward.
